title: Zone d'occupation des enfants
content:
Le dimanche 27 septembre, rejoignez-nous pour une Zone d'occupation des enfants, pour imaginer concrètement à quoi ressemblerait une société enfantiste, libérée de la domination des adultes, et s'organiser pour la faire advenir.


Les violences faites aux enfants sont partout


En juin dernier, le meurtre de Lyhanna, une enfant de 11 ans, nous a indigné·es et a renforcé notre détermination à éradiquer les violences sexistes et sexuelles, soi-disant grande cause nationale, en réalité préoccupation des seules organisations féministes. Les révélations d'inceste et de violences pédocriminelles dans cette affaire ont également rappelé la situation catastrophique des droits des enfants en France, sur laquelle les organisations enfantistes alertent depuis des années, sans réel changement politique.


Les violences contre les enfants et les adolescent·es sont pourtant bien plus répandues et ne font pas toujours les gros titres pour autant.


Des piscines crevées par la police dans les quartiers populaires en pleine canicule, à la mort au travail de lycéens et d'apprentis lors de stages professionnels, en passant par les violences au sein de l'Aide sociale à l'enfance, ou encore les enfants du Samu Social de Paris laissé·es à la rue cet été, la hausse de la mortalité infantile faute de services publics fonctionnels... La liste semble ne jamais s'arrêter.


La prison n'est pas la solution


Mettre les agresseurs en prison à perpétuité ne permet pas de réduire les violences. Donner davantage de moyens à la justice et à la police, qui protègent déjà l'ordre bourgeois, patriarcal, adultiste et raciste, non plus. Loin des appels au durcissement des peines et autres mesures répressives, nous pensons qu'il est plus qu'urgent de repenser radicalement la place des enfants dans notre société


Construire une société véritablement enfantiste


Pour cela, il faut imaginer concrètement à quoi ressemblerait une société enfantiste, libérée de la domination des adultes, et s'organiser pour la faire advenir.


C'est le projet de la

Zone d'Occupation des Enfants

 qui, le

dimanche 27 septembre sur la Place des Fêtes

, laissera le champ et l'espace libre aux enfants et aux ados, afin qu'elles et ils s'organisent, se forment (et s'amusent

 

!), loin de la violence et de l'ingérence des adultes.


Au programme :

 Assemblée générale des enfants

 Ateliers de formation et de pratique politique pour les enfants, ados et jeunes

 Des ateliers sportifs, créatifs et récréatifs

 Une cantine solidaire et un goûter

 Et un coin garderie pour les parents

 

!

Rejoignez-nous

author: Isaac Nellist
title: Students walk out of class again to protest Hanson’s racism and bigotry
content:
Thousands of high school and university students again walked out of class a second time to protest Pauline Hanson’s racism and bigotry on September 17. Rallies were held in 18 cities and towns across the country.

Students highlighted Hanson’s racist comments towards First Nations people and immigrants, her anti-LGBTIQ stance, her claim that domestic violence is a “two-way street” and her denial of the climate crisis.

Many pointed out that Hanson’s claim to be representing “ordinary Australians” is shown to be a lie because she is backed by Gina Rinehart, Australia’s richest person, and has consistently voted against pay rises and improved workers’ rights.

Students at the rally in Gadigal Country/Sydney told Green Left they did not support the vision for the country that Hanson is putting forward. “We’re the next generation of voters and we don’t want to see people like Pauline Hanson and One Nation who spread bigotry and hate in power,” one student said.

A year-12 student told Green Left he attended the protest to oppose Hanson’s racist rhetoric, and its adoption by Labor and the Coalition. “I’m here to stand in solidarity with women, immigrants, Palestinians, Indigenous people and queer people.”

Another student said they want politicians who are “for the people and not for billionaires”. “My mum is a person of colour and we don’t want someone who’s going to be racist.”

Atlas, an 18-year-old, said he came to the rally “because I am queer and people who I care about are in danger”.

Another told GL: “It’s hard to think that we could grow up in a future where someone like that could be deciding what happens in Australia. I think Pauline Hanson stands for racism, and I hate racism!”

Layla, from Newtown High, said she joined the rally to “stand against a monocultural Australia”.

“Australia is so much more interesting and multicultural, and to strip us of that would be to strip away everything good about this country.”

Grace Street, president of the University of Sydney Student Representative Council, told GL “high school and university students reject Hanson’s far-right politics”. “This is also a student issue — she just announced her plan to reduce the number of international students who come to the country and how many would be able to stay after they finish their degree.”

Rachel Evans, Socialist Alliance candidate for Heffron in the NSW elections in March, said it was exciting to see so many students campaigning against Hanson’s politics. “She is anti-refugee, anti-migrant, anti-trans and anti-woman, and it’s excellent to see young people start to organise.”

Another group of students told GL that Hanson’s beliefs are “destructive”. “Australia thrives off its multiculturalism and we’ll become the next laughing stock, after the US, if this continues.”

About 100 students joined the rally in Muloobinba/Newcastle. One student told GL they “don’t support what Hanson says about LGBTIQ people and people from other countries … this is a country that should be for everyone.

“She has no idea what she is doing and no idea what is right for the country or what we wants — she is totally out of touch.”

Another said Hanson was following the script of US President Donald Trump and his “Make America Great Again” movement.

[Join the speak-out against racism and bigotry in Glebe on September 26.]

title: Justice4Nzoy – gemeinsam gegen Rassismus und Polizei!
content:
Samstag, 12. September 2026, 14 Uhr Landesmuseum Zürich: Justice4Nzoy! Demonstration gegen Rassismus, Polizeigewalt und die Aufrüstung der Herrschenden.


Roger Nzoy Wilhelm wurde am 30. August 2021 von einem Polizisten erschossen. Sein Tod ist kein Einzelfall. Bei Polizeieinsätzen allein im Kanton Waadt wurden in den letzten Jahren auch Lamin Fatty, Hervé Mandundu, Mike Ben Peter, Michael Kenechukwu Ekemezie, die 14-jährige Camila und der 17-jährige Marvin getötet.


Rassistische Polizeigewalt hat System: Sie beginnt bei den Polizeischikanen, denen People of Color täglich ausgesetzt sind, und endet immer wieder bei tödlicher Gewalt. Der Kampf für Gerechtigkeit für Nzoy ist deshalb auch ein Kampf gegen alle Formen des staatlichen Rassismus.


Die diesjährige Demonstration steht im Zeichen der Militarisierung. Rassistische Polizeigewalt und die aktuelle Aufrüstung der Herrschenden gehören zusammen. So beruht der Kapitalismus auf der Ausbeutung von Ressourcen und Arbeitskraft – hier und besonders gewaltsam im globalen Süden. Für diese Ausbeutung benötigt er rassistische Gewalt, die von kolonialer Dominanz über die globale Ausbeutung bis zum hochgerüsteten Migrationsregime reicht. Der Genozid in Palästina zeigt aktuell, welche Brutalität die imperialistische Dynamik des Kapitalismus entfesseln kann.


In Europa schreitet die Militarisierung voran. In der kapitalistischen Krise verschärfen sich die gesellschaftlichen Widersprüche und der Staat setzt zur Sicherung seiner Interessen vermehrt auf militärische Gewalt: Kriege gegen aussen und Repression gegen innen. Rassismus ist dabei ein wichtiges Machtmittel. Zur Klassengesellschaft gehören nicht nur die Widersprüche zwischen herrschender und arbeitender Klasse, sondern auch rassistische Spaltungen innerhalb der ausgebeuteten Klasse. People of Color werden systematisch in prekäre Arbeitsverhältnisse gedrängt. Antimuslimischer Rassismus normalisiert den Genozid in Gaza und die Repression gegen die Palästina-Solidarität. Polizeigewalt setzt die Klassenherrschaft durch und wird dabei von rassistischer Ideologie gestützt.


Doch dieser Unterdrückung steht eine reiche Geschichte des Widerstands entgegen. In Europa reicht sie von migrantischem Widerstand an den Grenzen und in den Knästen bis zu Kämpfen gegen Polizeibrutalität wie der Kampagne für Oury Jalloh. In den USA verbinden sich die Erfahrungen der Black Panthers, der Black-Lives-Matter-Bewegung und des Widerstands gegen ICE. In all diesen Kämpfen zeigt sich die zentrale Bedeutung der Community-Arbeit: der Organisierung in den Quartieren und dem Aufbau solidarischer Strukturen. Von diesen Erfahrungen können wir lernen. Das beste Mittel gegen rassistische Gewalt ist Klassenkampf – von unten nach oben! Die Kampagne Justice4Nzoy greift diese Praxis auf, wenn sie sich im Kreis 4 und darüber hinaus vernetzt.


Organisieren wir antirassistische Solidarität in den Quartieren und Betrieben! Wehren wir uns, wenn unsere Angehörigen, Nachbar:innen, Freund:innen und Arbeitskolleg:innen von Polizei und Migrationsämtern bedroht, erniedrigt und angegriffen werden!


Schaffen wir widerständige Quartiere!

title: 50 Jahre Rock against Racism im Rückblick
content:
in der K9, Kinzigstraße 9 (Hinterhaus),


Berlin Friedrichshain, (Nähe U-Bahnhof Samariterstrasse)


Mittwoch, 16.09.2026, 19.30 Uhr


Runde Jahrestage werden ja eigentlich gern zur Identitätsvergewisserung genutzt. Etwas mag es da schon überraschen, dass es im Fall von 50 Jahre Punk, so der Eindruck nicht täuscht, doch eher ruhig geblieben ist. Sicher, auf arte und anderswo wird die für die Subkultur charakteristische rebellische Haltung abgefeiert und die üblichen Verdächtigen verlegen auf die musikalische Dimension fokussierte Erinnerungsliteratur. Blass bleiben hingegen die gesellschaftlichen Kontexte von Punk. Wir laden, mit dem bekannten Hintergrundbild des alten Clash-Promovideos zu ‚White Riot‘ aus dem Jahr 1976 im Hinterkopf, das randalierende Polizisten während des Notting Hill Carnivals im August 1976 zeigt, zu zwei kleinen Ausflügen in die ‚Kulissen‘.


Abend 1: White Riot? ‚Rock against Racism‘ im Rückblick


Who Shot the Sheriff? (Alan Miles, UK 2005, 66‘, OF)


Punk konstituierte sich im Moment einer tiefgreifenden Krise des fordistischen fixes in Großbritannien, in deren Rahmen erstmals in Europa, wenn wir von Italien mal absehen, rassistische und neofaschistische Kräfte wie die National Front bedrohlich an Raum in Politik, aber auch in Popular- und Jugendkultur zu gewinnen schienen. Hiergegen formierte sich ab Herbst 1976 von London ausgehend mit ‚Rock against Racism‘ eine Kampagne, die den Kampf auf dem Feld von Musik und (Jugend)Kultur selbst aufzunehmen trachtete und von Stuart Hall in seinem ersten Thatcherismus-Aufsatz „The Great Moving Right Show“ bereits 1979 als „one of the timeliest and best constructed of cultural interventions, repaying serious and extended analysis“ eingeschätzt wurde.


Alan Miles, im Hauptberuf bei der Londoner Feuerwehr beschäftigt, rekonstruierte die Geschichte der „Rock against Racism“- Kampagne der Jahre 1976/81 rückblickend im Moment ihrer Neuauflage unter dem Motto ‚Love Music Hate Racism‘ (2002) von ihrer Londoner Zentrale aus und mit Fokus auf die musikalische Dimension der Geschichte.


Zwar wurde die Kampagne in der BRD 1979/80 unter dem Motto ‚Rock gegen rechts‘ aufgegriffen, doch entwickelten sich diese Mobilisierungen in andere Richtungen; die wenigen deutschsprachigen Reflexionen zu RaR führen, von einem neueren Aufsatz von Gerd-Rainer Horn mal abgesehen, dementsprechend eher auf Abwege. Werfen wir also einen ersten Blick auf den Film (und vielleicht noch etwas Kleinkram) und schauen, was es mit RAR auf sich hatte, inwieweit die Geschichte noch relevant ist, was vielleicht davon gelernt werden könnte und ob es sich lohnen könnte, die Thematik zu einem späteren Zeitpunkt evt. noch einmal zu vertiefen.


(Beachtet bitte: Film in Englisch ohne Untertitel).

title: Nicht nur Pro Asyl warnt: In Syrien gibt es weder Schutz und Sicherheit noch dauerhaften Frieden
content:
Dossier


„Immer wieder kocht die öffentliche Debatte darüber hoch, ob der Krieg in Syrien nicht längst vorbei und das Land sicher genug für Abschiebungen ist. Ist es nicht. Jegliche Debatten über Rückkehr führen an der lebensgefährlichen Realität in Syrien vorbei. (…) Fakt ist, dass nahezu alle syrischen Flüchtlinge (99,8 %) vom Bundesamt für Migration und Flüchtlinge (BAMF) Schutz zugesprochen bekommen (…) Die enorm hohe Schutzquote spricht auch im achten Jahr des blutigen Syrien-Konflikts Bände. (…) Ein ähnliches Bild gibt es auch bei den Widerrufsverfahren  (…) Massive Kampfhandlungen finden in Syrien weiterhin statt. Die sich zunehmend verbreitende Auffassung, der Krieg sei fast zu Ende, ist falsch…“


Beitrag vom 25. September 2019 von und bei Pro Asyl


 – siehe immer noch dazu:


Bundesinnenminister Dobrindt will Schutzstatus von Syrern breitflächig aberkennen – auch wenn Syrien instabil und gefährlich ist


Bundesinnenminister will Schutzstatus von Syrern breitflächig aberkennen


„… Bundesinnenminister Alexander Dobrindt (CSU) will das Bundesamt für Migration und Flüchtlinge (Bamf) in Nürnberg noch in diesem Herbst anweisen, den Schutzstatus von Syrern auf breiter Front abzuerkennen. Das erfuhr das RedaktionsNetzwerk Deutschland (RND) von mehreren führenden CDU-Innenexperten im Bundestag. Der innenpolitische Sprecher der CDU/CSU-Bundestagsfraktion, Alexander Throm, sagte dem RND: „Beginnen sollte die Widerrufsprüfung bei allein reisenden jungen Männern, die Sozialhilfe beziehen, die also nicht arbeiten und dem Staat auf der Tasche liegen. Personen wie Ärzte oder Pfleger, die arbeiten, haben die Möglichkeit, in einen Arbeitsaufenthaltstitel zu wechseln.“ (…) Der CDU-Politiker fügte hinzu: „Parallel zum Widerruf braucht es ein besseres Programm zur Förderung der freiwilligen Rückkehr von syrischen Flüchtlingen. Das soll den Anreiz, freiwillig auszureisen, erhöhen. Denn jede freiwillige Ausreise ist billiger als eine zwangsweise Abschiebung.“ (…) Die „Neue Zürcher Zeitung“ hatte zuletzt berichtet, die Anweisung solle nach den Landtagswahlen in Berlin und Mecklenburg-Vorpommern erfolgen. Berichten zufolge lag die Zahl der Syrer, die Grundsicherung beziehen, im Frühjahr bei rund 450.000 – von weit über 900.000 Syrern insgesamt…“


Artikel von Markus Decker vom 21. September 2026 bei RND

 


PRO ASYL zur Debatte über Abschiebungen nach Syrien und den Widerruf des Schutzstatus: Syrien ist instabil und gefährlich


„

PRO ASYL kritisiert die Ankündigungen von Bundesinnenminister Alexander Dobrindt, dass sowohl Abschiebungen als auch geförderte Rückführungen nach Syrien ausgeweitet werden sollen.


Die Ankündigung von Bundesinnenminister Alexander Dobrindt, den Schutzstatus von immer mehr Syrer*innen aberkennen zu lassen und dabei insbesondere ‚alleinreisende junge Männer’ in den Blick zu nehmen, ist alarmierend. Über den Schutz eines Menschen entscheiden weder politische Zielvorgaben noch Fragen, ob jemand seinen Lebensunterhalt bestreiten kann – entscheidend ist die Situation und individuelle Gefährdung im Herkunftsland. Wer über Widerrufe und Abschiebungen nach Syrien spricht, muss zuvor über die Realität vor Ort sprechen. Und die ist nach wie vor instabil und gefährlich”, sagt Tareq Alaows, flüchtlingspolitischer Sprecher von PRO ASYL

…“

Pressemitteilung vom 22.09.2026


 mit Infors zur Lage in Syrien


Besuch von Ahmed al-Scharaa legitimiert dessen Herrschaft in Syrien, Warnungen vor Abschiebedeals ungehört, Kritik an Merz-Rückkehrforderungen immer lauter 


Syrien-Debatte von Merz: „Wie anmaßend ist es, Menschen als hin- und herschiebbare Masse zu betrachten?“ 


„

Was bezweckt Merz mit seiner Debatte über syrische Menschen, die in Deutschland ihren Lebensmittelpunkt haben? Interview mit Timmo Scherenberg vom Flüchtlingsrat.


Es ist nicht das erste Mal, dass Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz (CDU) mit einer Aussage eine unnötige Debatte vom Zaun bricht. Im aktuellen Fall betrifft es die Zukunft hier in Deutschland lebender Syrer:innen. Was ist das Ergebnis seines Vorstoßes – und was könnte Merz überhaupt damit bezwecken? author: Chiara Miraglia
title: What you need to know about the EU’s new digital deportation regime
content:
On 17 June, the European Parliament approved the new deportation law (called the “Return” Regulation) which aims to track undocumented people down and deport them from the EU in large numbers. The Regulation boosts the surveillance powers and digital control of national authorities and will rely heavily on technologies and data collection in their enforcement. This blog outlines the various digital tools and processes included in the EU’s new digital deportation regime.

By Protect Not Surveil (guest author) · September 23, 2026

On 17 June, the European Parliament approved the new EU’s deportation law (officially called the “Return” Regulation). The Deportation Regulation aims to track undocumented people down and deport them from the EU in large numbers. The most appalling of all the features of this new deportation system is the possibility for Member States to deport a person to a country they have never been to and detain them there indefinitely. More than 200 organisations petitioned against the legislative proposal, denouncing the new rules for what they are: inhumane.

The Regulation also boosts the surveillance powers and digital control of national authorities. Deportations rely heavily on technologies and data collection in their enforcement. At every step of the process, digital tools are used: to arrest and identify undocumented people, to detain them and restrict their movements, as well as to enforce deportation decisions.

The use of technologies severely undermine the digital and fundamental rights of people affected by this new regime, from data protection to asylum, dignity and liberty. The Deportation Regulation shows how migration and border control continue to serve as technological testing grounds for the EU and its Member States. They progressively but steadily widen the regime of exception at the core of the European data protection legal framework, and by doing so, irremediably undermine everyone’s fundamental rights.

The new deportation regime creates “obligations” on people without a valid residence or travel permit “to leave and cooperate”. To “promote” deportations and facilitate their identification, national authorities are authorised to take investigative measures, such as conducting home raids and searching any other “relevant premises” such as community centres, workplaces, hospitals, etc., force the collection of biometric data and search and seize personal belongings, electronic devices and “other items of relevance” – in other words literally anything from anyone. Further investigative measures defined under national law can also be deployed, which gives Member States a wide margin of discretion to introduce far-reaching ones.

Such practices codify the criminalisation of migrants and are disproportionate for migration management purposes. First, police raids without the requirement of independent judicial control in all EU countries will tarnish all places considered safe today and instill fear and insecurity among migrant communities and those providing services and support to them.

Second, coercion to collect biometric data, allegedly “as a last resort”, constitutes a grave infringement on the fundamental rights to dignity, integrity, liberty and security as it incentives the use of violence, punishment and detention. A 2018 report by Médecins du Monde showcased recurrent degrading treatments by Belgian police forces, sometimes amounting to torture (confinement in underwear in “freezer-cells”, blackmail, physical violence, etc.), against migrants in response to their refusal to give their fingerprints. The new provision allowing coercion is nothing less than a laissez-passer for further physical and psychological abuses.

Third, the search and seizure of electronic devices is extremely intrusive and manifestly disproportionate. Phone data extraction in particular can lead to the wide collection of sensitive data including data that is not necessarily relevant to the administrative procedure. In Germany, the Federal Administrative Court declared the Federal Office for Migration and Refugees’ (BAMF Migration Office) routine practice of searching asylum seekers’ mobile phones without cause unlawful. Seizing devices also encourages the procurement and use of hacking tools to bypass their security systems (pass-codes, PIN numbers, etc.), like Israeli company Cellebrite’s UFED (Universal Forensics Extraction Device), which can extract data even from locked smartphones in certain …

author: Unknown
title: Leonardo Caffo - Rethinking Lampedusa
content:
Author

: Leonardo Caffo

Title

: Rethinking Lampedusa

Subtitle

: Conceptual Architecture and the Philosophy of Europe’s Paradox

Date

: 2026

Source

: Anthropology (journal of) 2026


Abstract


 Lampedusa is habitually narrated as a site of emergency, yet its condition is structural rather than exceptional. This paper argues that the island functions as a paradox-object through which Europe’s constitutive contradictions become legible: geographically African, juridically European, and symbolically the very membrane that renders the two categories thinkable as distinct. Drawing on Foucault’s dispositif, Deleuze’s typology of continental and oceanic islands, and Achille Varzi’s distinction between fiat and bona fide boundaries, the paper shows that Lampedusa’s administrative and political borders systematically fail to coincide with its own geology — a mismatch condensed in the island’s municipal pairing with the volcanic, geologically European Linosa. Reading Agamben’s homo sacer against Hardt and Negri’s new barbarians, the paper treats the migrant not as a single, settled figure but as the site of two irreconcilable theoretical wagers, staged empirically in the recurring legal confrontation between Italian anti-NGO decrees and search-and-rescue obligations under international maritime law. Building on original fieldwork from the Rethinking Lampedusa research residency (2022–2025), the paper proposes reading the island as an anarchic object — a site where sovereignty is permanently held in default — and extends this default beyond the human register via Rosi Braidotti’s critical posthumanism, arguing that the same arche which excludes the migrant also subtends the human/non-human hierarchy visible in the island’s shared ecology of turtle nesting sites and disembarkation quays. The paper closes by proposing, through Rancière’s partage du sensible and Ariella Azoulay’s civil contract of photography, a counter-design for Lampedusa’s spatial and visual regime — one that would force the coexistence, rather than the segregation, of the island’s tourist and migrant economies. This remains, deliberately, an open rather than a concluding argument: further sections will need to test the proposal against concrete institutional and architectural alternatives.


 Keywords: Lampedusa; Linosa; new barbarians; fiat boundaries; Mediterranean migration; search and rescue; European Union border regime


Methodological Note: Practice-Based Research and the Position of the Author


 This paper departs, at several points, from the conventions of purely textual philosophical argument by drawing on material generated through Rethinking Lampedusa, a research and art-residency program the author has coordinated since 2022. It is necessary to state explicitly what kind of evidentiary status this material is being given, since practice-based research operates under different epistemic warrants than either empirical social science or textual exegesis, and conflating the three would misrepresent what is being claimed. The fieldwork referenced in Section 1.1 and elsewhere does not constitute ethnographic data in the disciplinary sense: it was not collected under a formal research protocol, does not involve systematic interviewing, coding, or triangulation, and makes no claim to generalizability beyond the specific, repeated, situated encounters it records. What it offers instead is what practice-based research literature has termed embodied and situated knowledge — insight generated through sustained, reflexive presence in a site, mediated by artistic and pedagogical practice (the residency’s Moleskine notebooks, workshops, and exhibitions) rather than by observation held at methodological arm’s length. This is a recognized, if still contested, mode of knowledge production within philosophy of art, aesthetics, and increasingly within border and migration studies, where scholars such as Federica Mazzara (cited throughout this paper) have similarly drawn on direct engagement with artistic and activist practice on Lampedusa itself to ground theoretical claims that pure textual analysis could not have generated independently.


 Three consequences follow from this status, and the reader should hold them in mind throughout.


 First, the fieldwork material functions in this paper as illustrative and generative, not as evidentiary in the sense a claim like “in April 2026, nineteen migrants died of hypothermia” is evidentiary, where the latter is …

author: Sharon Zhang
title: ICE “Disappears” Thousands Ordered to Be Deported From Detainee Locator
content:
This could make it “nearly impossible” for some people to challenge their deportation orders, an attorney said.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is removing the names of its detainees who are facing final deportation orders from its public online database.

The move will disrupt detainees’ legal challenges to deportation and leave their whereabouts unknown to their lawyers and loved ones.

The agency quietly removed thousands of people from its online detainee locator on September 15, the Associated Press reports. Certain detention facilities will not be subject to the new order if judges have ruled that they are required to list detainees in their facilities.

The exact number of names removed is unclear, but judges have issued over 740,000 removal and voluntary departure orders this year, while reports have found that ICE arrested nearly 16,000 people in July who were subject to final removal orders. Experts and advocates have criticized the practice as digitally “disappearing” immigrants, saying that it’s yet another erosion of due process rights.

The agency has also issued a new policy barring immigration officials from sharing the locations of such detainees, two former Department of Homeland Security officials told The Washington Post.

This policy of hiding detainees’ locations will make it far harder or “nearly impossible” for many people to challenge their removals, legal experts said, as the agency rushes to make quotas for its mass deportation campaign.

American Civil Liberties Union Senior Staff Attorney My Khanh Ngo told AP that eight Somali men, her clients, detained at the U.S.’s Guantanamo Bay detention camp are among those whose names were removed. She said that such a move could make it “nearly impossible” to challenge many deportation cases.

“If you can’t find your client, don’t know what’s happening to your client, you can’t get that information to the court to stop their removal,” said Ngo.

“Families are freaking out because they think the person has been deported and they don’t know where the person might be,” said Greg Chen, senior director of government relations for the American Immigration Lawyers Association, per AP. “On the attorney side, this has serious implications for the ability to contact their client. It certainly has implications about how it will interfere with the attorney-client relationship.”

ICE has already faced scrutiny over its practices of quietly transferring detainees to different facilities without notification, often leaving families terrified when they find out that their loved one has been moved thousands of miles away.

Over the past year, the Trump administration has sent over 25,000 people to countries that they had no previous connection with, according to Refugees International. Under the direction of White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, the Trump administration transformed a former refugee bureau within the State Department into the “Office of Remigration,” which has authorized or pledged $410 million in agreements with 31 countries, mostly in Africa and Latin America.

The news of the database deletions comes just days after an ICE agent shot and wounded a Venezuelan man, Wilber Garcés Pérez, in Austin over the weekend. ICE has reportedly transferred Garcés from a local hospital to a detention facility against doctors’ recommendations, as doctors have not removed the bullet from his body because it is too close to his spine. Despite this, a judge has ordered the 28-year-old DoorDash driver to be present for an in-person deportation hearing on September 30.

author: Sophia Cope
title: D.C. Circuit Must Vacate a Drone Flight Restriction That Criminalized Recording Immigration Agents
content:
EFF joined an

amicus brief

 with ACLU, ACLU of D.C., National Press Photographers Association, and Professional Photographers of America to urge the D.C. Circuit to vacate an FAA drone flight restriction that violated the

First Amendment right to record law enforcement

. This is an important case—

Levine v. FAA

—challenging the ability of the government to punish drone pilots who record law enforcement officers engaged in official business.

 


As we wrote about

earlier this year

, the FAA issued a flight restriction for drones that had effectively criminalized the recording of Department of Homeland Security officers, including immigration agents from ICE and CBP, and their vehicles (what the FAA called “mobile assets” including “ground vehicle convoys and their associated escorts”) even if the drone was over half a mile away.

 


A drone operator, represented by the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press,

sued the FAA in March

 [PDF]. But in April, the

FAA rescinded the flight restriction

.

 


The petitioner argued in his

opening brief

 that the court should evaluate the legality of the flight restriction even though it was withdrawn. Drone pilots could still be punished for violations that occurred when the flight restriction was in effect. And the FAA could reinstate the flight restriction at any time, given that the rescission did not seem to reflect “a true change of heart” but rather an effort by the agency to avoid judicial review.

 


The amicus brief, filed in support of the petitioner, noted that drones are unique because they provide “perspectives that cannot be captured by ground-based imagery,” and they “are far more maneuverable than ground-level cameras, and they are both much cheaper and much safer than using a chartered plane or helicopter to record newsworthy events from above.” The brief highlighted that drones have captured “bird’s-eye images of protest activity” and “police uses of force against protestors,” and have “allowed journalists to provide the public with up-to-the-minute information about natural disasters without putting themselves in harm’s way.”

 


The brief argued that using drones to capture images and video is information-gathering activity protected by the First Amendment (similar to using

cell phones to record law enforcement

). The brief also argued that the FAA’s flight restriction appeared to be issued specifically to ban the recording of immigration agents and thus hinder accountability for their enforcement actions—it surely wasn’t a coincidence that the FAA imposed “no-drone zones around all roving DHS patrols just as those patrols were provoking intense national backlash.” If that’s true, it would make the FAA’s action a content-based restriction on speech that is subject to strict scrutiny—the highest First Amendment standard—and presumptively unconstitutional. And even under less rigorous standards of First Amendment scrutiny, the flight restriction is unconstitutional because the FAA can’t articulate any valid governmental interest justifying such a sweeping restriction on speech.

 


Resolving this issue to protect First Amendment rights is especially urgent as government agencies continue to

sink billions of dollars

 into technology designed to counter drones—technology that could easily be deployed against journalists and other people hoping to use drones to document government abuse. 

 


We urge the D.C. Circuit to review the petition and to vacate the FAA’s flight restriction, which would send a message that the government can’t avoid accountability by punishing those who exercise their First Amendment rights.

author: webdev@democracynow.org (Democracy Now!)
title: "Extraordinary Rendition All Over Again": U.S. Deportees Sent to Equatorial Guinea Beaten, Imprisoned
content:
Two men deported from the United States to Equatorial Guinea were arrested by local police forces and transferred to a prison earlier this month, in apparent retaliation for speaking out about conditions they faced in the Central African country. Samson Birhane, who is from Eritrea, and Ahmed Soliman, a gay asylum seeker from Egypt, were both deported by the Trump administration despite U.S. immigration courts granting them protections.


On September 11, police forces arrived at Hotel Bamy in the city of Malabo, where more than two dozen people have been confined after their deportation from the United States to Equatorial Guinea, a country they have no ties to, as part of President Trump’s secretive

“third-country” agreements

. Birhane and Soliman say they were arrested and taken to prison for speaking out about the inhumane conditions endured by U.S. deportees at the hotel and threats by armed forces. While confined at the hotel, U.S. deportees have decried denial of medical care and legal assistance, and abuses they’ve described as psychological torture.


“Starting in November 2025, … the United States started this horrendous policy of sending immigrants not from Equatorial Guinea to Equatorial Guinea, a country that the U.S. knows very, very well that is a human rights violator,” says human rights lawyer Tutu Alicante. “The State Department reports that the U.S. has been putting out for the last three decades are consistent about the fact that Equatorial Guinea uses torture, uses incommunicado detentions, and often extrajudicial killings of people that it keeps in prison.”

author: Unknown
title: Митинг и демонстрация в Хельсинки против депортаций
content:
Мы публикуем отчёт о мероприятии, прошедшем в Финляндии в эту субботу. Автор - антифашист Олег Волин.

В Хельсинки прошли митинг и демонстрация против депортации российских беженцев и противников войны в Украине.

19 сентября в 14:00 на площади около железнодорожного вокзала Хельсинки прошел митинг против враждебной политики миграционной службы Финляндии, которая необоснованно высылает россиян противников войны, сбежавших от репрессий в РФ, обратно в руки олигархического путинского режима.

В начале митинга собралось около 50 человек, среди них были представители анархистской группы «А-ryhmä», антифашисты, молодежь из нескольких левых организаций Хельсинки (Helsinki Left Youths, SitVas), правозащитники, либеральные и ЛГБТ активисты, активисты демократического сообщества русскоязычных, союза отказчиков от оружия, Queer Asylum Finland, движения «Еда вместо бомб».

Выступили один активист и один беженец из России, они рассказали про удручающую ситуацию с получением убежища в Финляндии для русскоязычных беженцев, многие люди вынуждены ждать годами решения от миграционной службы, эти решения в подавляющем большинстве бывают негативными, несмотря на то, что люди занимались какой-то политической деятельностью в РФ и серьезно опасаются возвращаться обратно из-за угрозы репрессий и посадки в тюрьму.

Затем прошла демонстрация по центральным улицам Хельсинки, в ходе которой участники растянули транспарант «Нет — депортациям, беженцы — добро пожаловать!» и скандировали: «Если вы выступаете против войны, вас нельзя депортировать!», «Если Мигри прогонит — Путин поблагодарит вас!», «Скажи это громко, скажи это четко, беженцам здесь рады!» и другие речёвки.

После этого, в 15:00, на площади Наринкатори около станции метро Камппи прошел еще один митинг. Собралось около 70 человек. Выступили ещё около трое беженцев россиян и несколько активистов правозащитных организаций. Они поделились своими историями о тяжёлой ситуации с получением убежища в Финляндии, кто-то из выступающих плакал от нахлынувших чувств. Выступавшие говорили, что бояться возвращаться обратно в РФ, где их ждут неминуемые проблемы с полицией и спецслужбами, что они хотят остаться в Финляндии, жить в спокойной обстановке без угрозы из жизни.

Активисты раздавали прохожим листовки о сути проблемы и требованиях к миграционной службе. Также во время и после митинга на Наринкатори была организована раздача еды от двух групп «Еда вместо бомб Хельсинки». Участники могли бесплатно подкрепиться кофе с выпечкой и другой едой. Акция прошла в хорошей и доброжелательной атмосфере, без провокаций и проблем со стороны полиции.

Полный фотоотчёт смотрите по ссылке.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Will New Changes Improve Taiwan’s Image on Migrant Work?
content:
A NUMBER OF changes are set to occur in the migrant work landscape in Taiwan going forward.

For one, the first batch of migrant workers in the hospitality field has arrived, consisting of 35 Indonesians. These 35 workers arrived in Taiwan as part of the new Multinational Skilled Worker Enhancement Program and are classified as skilled labor, rather than blue-collar migrant workers. The 35 workers previously conducted internships in Taiwan of at least one year in length and are required to reach A-2 level listening and speaking within three years, per the requirements of the program.

Their employer, Regent Taipei, previously hired them as interns, and it approached them individually under the new program. The 35 workers are mostly in their twenties and will return to the departments they worked in. The terms of the new program specify that hospitality industry businesses can hire a new migrant worker if they increase the salary of their lowest-paid Taiwanese worker by 2,000 NT, though hiring of migrant workers is still capped at 10% of the workforce.

The hospitality industry, which has a shortfall of 6,000 workers annually, has long clamored for hiring migrant workers to take up positions that Taiwanese are no longer interested in working. At the same time, it had already gradually been the case that what were technically internships had become a means of hiring migrant workers in the hospitality industry. The government seems to now be making moves at regulation, which hopefully can provide workers with stronger protections.

One notes that the new batch of workers will not pay recruitment fees, as instituting zero-fee recruitment practices as Taiwan has long been called on to do. Likewise, Taiwan is set to open a direct hiring desk in the Philippines in the near future, as another means of instituting recruitment that routes around the brokers that traditionally have imposed heavy fees on migrant workers to arrange for their transportation to and from Taiwan and their employment after arriving. The direct hiring desk mandates that employers cover travel to and from Taiwan.

Clearly, Taiwan is aiming to clean up its international image, given increased scrutiny on migrant worker abuses. The pressure to institute zero-fee recruitment is largely external and is a direct result of Taiwan agreeing to such terms in trade negotiations with the US.

Indeed, similarly, Taiwan has built new facilities for migrant workers in the Cianjhen Fishing Port to the tune of 8.2 billion NT. Such facilities are intended to provide showers, laundry, WiFi, and hotel services for migrant workers, especially as labor abuses against migrant fishermen and the poor working conditions they face have increasingly seen scrutiny in past years. But despite the expenditure, the facility has been criticized, as migrant workers in many cases cannot afford the hotel facilities, which require 1,000 NT per day. Likewise, the facility has insufficient showers and laundry machines, often leading migrant workers to go elsewhere. It is to be seen whether the government’s recent actions on the migrant work front prove to be simply an attempt to whitewash their poor treatment, then, with token gestures done for the sake of appearance that mean little in terms of concrete change.

author: Mebratu Kelecha
title: The Rivalry Between Ethiopia and Eritrea Is Reshaping Tigray
content:
On 1 August 2026, Ethiopian federal and Tigrayan forces clashed in western Tigray, a northern Ethiopian region bordering Eritrea and Sudan.  By 3 August, fighting had subsided, but

hundreds of Tigrayans, including wounded fighters, had crossed into war-torn Sudan

. The clash followed Ethiopia’s 1 June election: Tigray did not vote, while Prime Minister

Abiy Ahmed’s Prosperity Party won 438 seats

.


Tigray’s 2020–2022 war followed a power struggle between Abiy and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which governed Tigray and dominated Ethiopia’s ruling coalition until Abiy took office in 2018. Eritrean and Amhara forces supported the federal government.

An African Union-brokered agreement signed in Pretoria in November 2022

 ended large-scale fighting and provided for disarmament, restored services and an interim administration pending elections.


Those alliances have since shifted.

Ethiopia’s government alleges cooperation

 among Eritrea, the TPLF faction led by party chairman Debretsion Gebremichael, and elements of Fano, a network of Amhara militias whose fighters once supported Abiy but now fight his government. Eritrea and the TPLF deny cooperation.

Ethiopia also accused Eritrea of occupying

its territory and backing

armed groups

.

Eritrea

denied the charges.


The 2018 Ethiopia–Eritrea peace agreement made joint war in Tigray easier than lasting cooperation on borders and trade. The breakdown in relations reshaped outside support for rival Tigrayan factions.

Pretoria left

territory and authority unresolved. Control of government funding, gold mines, border routes and armed forces helps rival leaders hold power, while residents have little say.


Two presidents, no public mandate


After the Pretoria agreement, Abiy reportedly vetoed Debretsion as interim

president. TPLF official Getachew Reda became interim president after an internal party ballot. Residents had no vote in either process.


In March 2025,

Debretsion’s faction pushed Getachew aside. Abiy then appointed Tadesse Worede, commander of the Tigray Defence Forces (TDF), the region’s wartime

army. Abiy extended Tadesse’s

tenure in April 2026

.

In

May, the TPLF revived the

regional

council elected in Tigray’s 2020 vote

, which the federal government had rejected. The council elected Debretsion regional president. Tadesse maintained his claim.


Ethiopia’s government controls federal funding, official recognition and superior military resources; Debretsion’s camp controls much of Tigray’s party organisation, regional administration and armed forces. The federal government cites Pretoria to extend an unelected administration. The TPLF cites its 2020 mandate. Neither asked Tigrayans who should govern them now


War-damaged homes in Werkamba, Tigray, 2020: Jnyssen


This is also a struggle over post-war resources.

The International Crisis

Group


reports that senior TDF officers have

business

interests in Tigray’s gold

mines

and that factions have contested control of the Endowment Fund for the Rehabilitation of Tigray

, a large party-linked business group. Federal funding, salaries and mining revenue help finance rival authorities.


Getachew, now Abiy’s adviser, joined an alliance with members of the Tigray Peace Force, a TDF splinter

militia. The German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP)

says this force appears to receive federal ammunition, food and pay.


In July 2026,

Human Rights Watch documented abductions and unlawful recruitment by Tigrayan authorities, including

of

children as young as

fifteen. The

TPLF denied forced recruitment.


How allies became enemies


The

July 2018 Joint Declaration

, signed by Abiy and Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki, ended hostility after their 1998–2000 border war and promised cooperation. Reopened contacts helped divided families and traders. Yet it established no publicly accountable rules for

trade, currency exchange,

land or border crossings

.

author: Fozzie
title: Chapter 31: The Genesis of the Industrial Capitalist
content:
Harry Cleaver's study guide to chapter 31 of Marx's Capital volume 1.

The wealth that financed the rise of industry, Marx emphasizes, was not accumulated through frugality

Colonialism: Marx: Dutch, English, Spanish

Public Debt: one of the earliest and longest lasting mechanisms that Marx discusses

Trade Protection: monopolization of trade and the extorsion of heavy taxes combine in the use of:

These methods financed industrialization

"If money," Marx concludes, "'comes into the world with a congenital blood-stain on one cheek,' capital comes dripping from head to toe, from every pore, with blood and dirt." (p.926)

Industrial capital, the prototypical form of capital, emerged alongside agrarian capitalism. Marx refutes the myth that this emergence was accomplished purely through conscientious frugality and entrepreneurial investment by describing the actual sources of finance for investment that became permanent features of capitalism, well beyond the early period of primitive accumulation.

Marx’s attack on the myth of entrepreneurial frugality remains important because the myth still flourishes. It became foundational to the ideology of upward mobility, which claims that anyone who works hard can move up the income hierarchy, even to the very top. Recently, it has been refurbished as part of the right-wing attack on those roles of the state used by workers for their own protection. In the United States, amidst the crisis of Keynesianism in the 1970s, this ideology was elaborated by neo-conservatives, and soon became known in the rest of the world by the label neoliberalism.(1) In the Global South, it has been an important element of the writings of people such as economists P. T. Bauer (1915–2002)—created a "life peer" by the UK's union busting Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher!—and Hernando De Soto Polar (1841 -)&mdashbest known for his counter-revolutionary(2) advocacy of government deregulation—both of whom have been vociferous advocates of "liberating" the market and entrepreneurship around the world. In the Soviet Bloc and China, the appeal to liberate entrepreneurial spirit was a part of the reformist attack on state planning, and after the fall of the wall, the imposition of the market and the gutting of worker protectons became integral parts of the programs of "shock therapy" reforms in Eastern Europe.

While Marx accepts the grain of truth that many small guild masters, independent small artisans and even wage-laborers, “transformed themselves. . . into capitalists.”(3), he argues that such personal initiative, savings and investment were not the major mechanisms by which industrial capitalism emerged. Nor we can add, are small businesses today the major source of capitalist expansion.

Since the 1970s, attacks on the Keynesian social and environmental programs and regulations have been rationalized by the pretense that they undermine entrepreneurship. State paternalism, neoliberals have claimed, whether of welfare state in the West or of socialist governments in the East, creates dependency and tends to snuff out the entrepreneurial spirit vital to the building of free enterprise and society more generally. Targets have included programs that support working-class income and increase workers' ability to resist exploitation, as well as environmental, occupational safety and health regulations that workers have imposed on business to limit damage to both humans and the rest of nature. Neoliberals call for deregulation to cut corporate costs and enhance private profits, the selling off (enclosure) of public lands for purposes of exploitation, the removal of environmental regulations to encourage investment, the reduction or elimination of social safety-net programs, vouchers to finance private schools outside the public-school system, and in countries now freed from Soviet-style regimes, the substitution of private farming for state or collective farms. Hypocrisy is blatant in the steadfast opposition these same capitalist apologists maintain to any reduction in the role of government in the defense and subsidization of corporations and in their repeated support for "supply-side" tax cuts that supposedly increase investment but actually benefit the wealthy at the expense of everyone else. Such policies have rightly given rise to the term "corporate welfare."

Analyzing the rise of industrial capitalism shows us how these arguments are just as ideological and self-serving as those Marx confronted in …

author: CNT Santander
title: Crónica de la charla de Andrew Gartzea
content:
El pasado viernes 18 de septiembre, nuestras compañeras del GT de Feminismos tuvieron el placer de presentar a Andrew Gartzea con su charla sobre la

queerización

 en nuestra sede de CNT Santander.


Acudieron un montón de personas bonitas a

hackear

 la normalidad y vivieron una velada increíble.


Nos cuentan cómo fue la experiencia y de qué trató la charla.


Escrito por Orsa


LA QUEERIZACIÓN DE LO COTIDIANO


«¿Qué harías si desapareciera el capitalismo?» es la pregunta con la que Andrew nos reta a imaginar un mundo anti-normativo. Algunes quieren reconectar con la naturaleza («me tiraría en el bosque»), otres lo conjugan con el placer («iría a la playa desnuda») y no pueden faltar les que abordan la dimensión del cuidado («viviría con mi pareja y haríamos una biblioteca, incluso podríamos dar clases» o «haría ropa para todos los cuerpos»). Por su lado, servidore lo tiene claro: seguiría apoyando estas acciones de formación y reflexión revolucionaria autogestionadas.


«Hacer» es, en resumen, el verbo que vertebra la exposición. Andrew se opone al «ser», cuestiona el movimiento identitario y sus repercusiones segregacionistas recordándonos un uso del término

queer

 paraguas, intencionalmente ambiguo, capaz de acogernos a todes les que estamos en contra del patriarcado y el capital. Revisa la historia y genealogías de lo

queer

, el patriarcado y el capitalismo en busca de la ontología de las opresiones a través no solo de la exposición académica de autores como Butler, Anzaldua, Esteban Muñoz o Foucault, sino también de sus propias vivencias como persona transgénero y migrante en Reino Unido («La isla de las TERF»). Desde un enfoque marxista, la charla nos demuestra cómo el capitalismo está dispuesto a perpetrar cualquier masacre con tal de no desaparecer y ha ido evolucionando su sistema moral hasta fenómenos como la sociedad del cansancio (Byung-Chul Han), la modernidad líquida de Bauman, o el «

n-word

» (ingenio con el que Andrew se refiere al neoliberalismo). Frente a la pesimista cita celebre de Mark Fisher, «es más fácil imaginar el fin del mundo que el fin del capitalismo», Andrew nos arroja esperanza con su «todo lo que tiene un origen tiene un final, incluido el capitalismo»; pero la utopía (anarquista, queer, transfeminista, decolonial, antirracista, anticapacitista, antiespecista) no será un horizonte visible si no performamos diariamente lo utópico, es decir, si desafiamos la norma.


Termino esta breve nota invitándoos a seguir aprendiendo a través del Instagram de Andrew (@andrewgartzea) o el libro del que es coautor: Trans/bordes — Nuevas líneas para el pensamiento trans* (Ed. Kaótica libros).

author: anonerror
title: Después de la derrota: organización y lucha
content:
Después de la derrota: organización y lucha

El primer gran ciclo revolucionario mundial, desplegado entre 1917 y 1919, y el segundo gran ciclo de luchas proletarias, cuyo momento culminante se situó entre finales de los años sesenta y la segunda mitad de los setenta, fueron dos grandes momentos de constitución y combate del proletariado internacional. Entre ambos se produjeron derrotas decisivas, transformaciones profundas del capitalismo, modificaciones sustanciales de la composición de clase y nuevas formas de organización y de lucha. Comprender lo que ocurrió después de aquellas derrotas constituye una de las tareas fundamentales de cualquier reflexión contemporánea sobre la revolución social.

El problema que atraviesa toda discusión actual sobre la revolución no consiste en averiguar si el proletariado existe todavía como una figura idéntica a la que conocieron Marx, Bakunin, Luxemburg o los revolucionarios de comienzos del siglo XX. La cuestión verdaderamente importante consiste en comprender qué ha ocurrido con aquella forma histórica de constitución de la clase y qué posibilidades pueden abrirse después de su derrota.

El movimiento obrero clásico, entendido como el largo ciclo histórico durante el cual el proletariado se constituyó progresivamente como fuerza social, política y cultural diferenciada, puede situarse aproximadamente entre las revoluciones de 1848 y la profunda crisis de las formas obreras tradicionales que se desarrolló entre los años setenta y ochenta del siglo XX. No se trata, evidentemente, de fechas mágicas ni de una frontera absoluta: el movimiento obrero no nació completamente formado en 1848 y tampoco desapareció de golpe en 1980. Se trata de identificar un ciclo histórico en el que determinadas formas de composición de clase, organización, conciencia y lucha alcanzaron una estabilidad suficiente para constituir una fuerza social reconocible y relativamente permanente.

Durante más de un siglo, ese movimiento creó sindicatos, partidos, consejos, sóviets, asociaciones, cooperativas, ateneos, escuelas, milicias, sociedades de socorro mútuo, organizaciones de solidaridad, comunidades obreras, organizaciones revolucionarias y múltiples formas de sociabilidad. Estas instituciones no fueron simples instrumentos exteriores a una clase ya constituida, sino expresiones concretas de una determinada composición histórica del proletariado. El movimiento obrero no se limitó a luchar dentro de las relaciones sociales existentes: creó también espacios propios de reproducción de la vida, formas de cultura, mecanismos de solidaridad y organizaciones capaces de transmitir experiencias de una generación a otra. Cuando aquella composición comenzó a desarticularse, no desapareció el proletariado: lo que desapareció fue una determinada manera histórica de existir políticamente como proletariado.

Las revoluciones de 1848 representan un momento fundamental de esta constitución histórica porque hicieron visible al proletariado moderno como fuerza social diferenciada y colocaron en el centro de la lucha la cuestión de la emancipación de los trabajadores. A partir de entonces se desarrolló un proceso contradictorio de acumulación de experiencias, derrotas, victorias parciales, organizaciones y formas de conciencia que permitió a millones de trabajadores reconocerse como pertenecientes a una misma clase, pese a las enormes diferencias nacionales, profesionales, culturales y políticas que los separaban.

La Primera Internacional, la Comuna de París, el crecimiento del sindicalismo, las organizaciones socialistas y anarquistas, las grandes huelgas de masas, las revoluciones de comienzos del siglo XX, la Revolución rusa, la revolución alemana de 1918-1919, las insurrecciones obreras europeas, la revolución española de 1936 y las grandes luchas obreras de la segunda mitad del siglo XX pertenecen a ese largo proceso, aunque entre ellas existieran diferencias profundas y, en ocasiones, antagonismos irreconciliables.

La historia del movimiento obrero no fue, por tanto, una marcha lineal hacia una forma definitiva de organización. Fue una sucesión de experiencias históricas en las que los trabajadores tuvieron que inventar, adaptar y abandonar formas organizativas según las condiciones concretas de la lucha. El sindicato, el partido, el consejo, la asamblea, el comité, la organización de fábrica, la cooperativa, la organización revolucionaria y otras muchas formas de asociación respondieron a situaciones históricas …

author: Monthly Review Press
title: Forthcoming! “Grand Theft Capital”, by Fred Magdoff and John Bellamy Foster
content:
A

New York Times

 headline in early 2026 announced what many workers have known for years: “For Many Cash-Strapped Americans, ‘Basic Living has become a Burden.’” Living paycheck-to-paycheck, with little or no savings for emergencies, workers are struggling to make ends meet. It should come as no surprise that, without a clear sense of the problem’s source, workers are left blaming easy targets: immigrants, people of color, religious minorities, or damaging decisions by a few, corporate bad apples.


But as

Grand Theft Capital

demonstrates, workers’ current conditions are the result of a deliberate, long-term effort by the corporate rich to increase their own wealth largely by extracting it from workers’ pockets. The evidence shows that workers’ wages have not kept pace with rising costs and that they’re feeling unhappy and stressed on the job. This partly reflects the weakening of worker power as union membership has declined over the past sixty years—reaching levels last seen before the major unionization wave of the 1930s. Regardless of what mainstream economists and the Consumer Price Index suggest, successive generations of young workers have been confronting difficult and precarious employment conditions. On top of it all, workers of all generations are alarmed at the possibility of job obsolescence given the looming threat of AI and automation.


In the face of this evidence,

Grand Theft Capital

 offers a clear answer to the source of the problem and charts a clear way forward. What workers are facing is nothing less than a class war waged from above; the only solution is an equally determined class war from below.

author: Publicación Abierta
title: La URSS venció al nazismo: lo de Hollywood son cuentos
content:
Qué fue el nazismo.


El nazismo se basaba, y se basa, en una supuesta supremacía racial y en la necesidad de un «espacio vital» para Alemania, que le permitiera robar los recursos de otros países y esclavizar a sus gentes mediante guerras de conquista. Empezó matando a su propio pueblo: por discapacidad, por ser homosexual, gitano o judío, o por ser comunista. Es una teoría del odio, de la superioridad racial y del abuso de todo aquel considerado inferior. En Europa añadió a su genocidio ideológico un genocidio racial y devastó el continente en la Segunda Guerra Mundial.


El frente oriental.


Fue el comunismo, fue la URSS, quien venció al nazismo y al fascismo. Solo con la invasión de la Unión Soviética en 1941, Alemania desplegó unas 154 divisiones. El frente oriental fue el mayor y más mortífero de la guerra, y allí murieron en torno al 73 % de los soldados alemanes caídos en toda la contienda. Allí fue aplastada la maquinaria militar nazi por el Ejército Rojo. En el frente occidental, tras el desembarco de Normandía en 1944, Alemania mantenía unas 76 divisiones frente a británicos, estadounidenses, franceses, canadienses y otros aliados. Nadie discute el esfuerzo de los aliados occidentales, pero los números hablan por sí solos.


Un precio brutal.


¿Qué quiero decir con esto? Que la Unión Soviética fue quien cargó con el mayor peso de la guerra y que, además, sufrió el mayor castigo y pagó un precio brutal en vidas humanas y en destrucción. Un pueblo obrero y campesino se levantó contra la barbarie y la derrotó. Esa es una verdad que quieren enterrar quienes prefieren que creamos que aquella victoria fue de otros.


Lo que no cuenta Hollywood.


Durante décadas, el cine de Hollywood nos ha contado la guerra a su medida: desembarcos, soldados estadounidenses, héroes de rostro conocido y final feliz en las playas de Normandía. Se ha repetido tanto que mucha gente cree de buena fe que la guerra se decidió allí. No es casualidad. Tras 1945, en plena Guerra Fría, la industria cultural del bloque capitalista tenía todo el interés en borrar del relato al Ejército Rojo. Stalingrado, Kursk, el cerco de Leningrado o la toma de Berlín apenas existen en el imaginario popular de Occidente, pese a que allí se decidió el destino de Europa. Quien cuenta la historia decide quién la ganó y, por eso, la clase trabajadora tiene que recuperar también su relato. Lo de Hollywood son cuentos; los datos, no.


Dos ideologías enemigas.


Segundo: ¿cómo se puede comparar y poner al mismo nivel dos ideologías contrapuestas y enemigas, que buscan modelos de sociedad opuestos y defienden los intereses de clases enfrentadas? Quienes comparan el nazismo con el comunismo lo hacen por ignorancia o, peor, de forma intencionada, para engañar a la gente y lanzar bulos. El comunismo defiende los intereses de la clase trabajadora, la igualdad, el antirracismo y el internacionalismo. El nazismo y el fascismo son los perros de guerra del capitalismo en tiempos de crisis sistémica o de despertar de los pueblos: racistas, clasistas y nacionalistas en el peor de los sentidos.


Qué es el comunismo.


El comunismo es una ideología basada en la recuperación de los medios de producción, la energía y los sectores estratégicos para ponerlos en manos y al servicio de la clase trabajadora, y acabar así con la explotación y con la acumulación de riqueza de una oligarquía minoritaria. Un comunista es quien piensa que toda persona, por el hecho de nacer, tiene derecho a una vida digna y a tener cubiertas sus necesidades básicas; que la economía debe estar al servicio del ser humano y no al revés; que trabajamos para vivir y no vivimos para trabajar; que la patria es la clase obrera, y que la solidaridad, la igualdad, la fraternidad y la justicia social son los cimientos de un futuro socialista.


El capitalismo, el genocida más respetado.


Frente a eso, el capitalismo mata de hambre, mata en guerras de expolio de recursos, masacra pueblos y pobres, esclaviza a millones de hombres, mujeres y niños. Y, curiosamente, sigue siendo el genocida más respetado de la historia. En el capitalismo, el ser humano está al servicio de la economía y la vida no vale nada.


El modelo social y económico comunista es mucho más humano e igualitario que las democracias capitalistas y es el antagonista natural del fascismo. Lo decía Einstein: la única forma de eliminar los graves males del mundo es una economía socialista, acompañada de un sistema educativo orientado a metas …

title: Confederación Nacional del Trabajo - Ceuta, Morocco and the Weaponisation of the Working Class
content:
Author

: Confederación Nacional del Trabajo

Title

: Ceuta, Morocco and the Weaponisation of the Working Class

Date

: 3 August 2026

Source

: Retrieved on 21

st

 September 2026 from

www.iclcit.org


 First of all, we’d like to state our solidarity with the families and friends of all those who have died and those who are imprisoned.


 The recent tensions between the Spanish and Moroccan states have once again placed Ceuta at the centre of a conflict which is being presented as a matter of national sovereignty and border control. However, we at the CNT believe that this approach obscures the real problem and diverts attention away from those who suffer the consequences: the working class from both sides of the border.


The governments of Spain and Morocco use the border as a tool for political bargaining.

 The Moroccan state uses control over migration flows as a means of exerting diplomatic pressure and to extract concessions to the dictatorship of Mohammed VI, and the Spanish one responds by stepping up the militarisation of the borders and tightening immigration policies (‘outsourcing’ the deadly border policy).


 This concessions include the legitimisation of the king’s dictatorial regime, with its hundreds of political prisoners and disregard for international rules, or the acceptance of its military occupation of Western Sahara, with its trail of human rights violations. Trapped in the midst of this dispute between states are the thousands of workers forced to migrate due to political repression, poverty, precarious living conditions, lack of opportunities, or the consequences of a deeply unequal economic model. It is this inequality that creates borders. Without it, there would be no ‘border’.


 This situation is exploited by the far right, which singles out migration as the root cause of all social problems. The fact that the arrival of migrants has become an international spectacle is a political decision made by the big capital and its governments.


 In this regard, there is a clear de facto alliance between the xenophobic far right – which defends the capitalists and scapegoats the migrants – and the dictatorship of the king of Morocco, who, as we have seen, cares very little for his own people. It is no coincidence that, just a few days ago, the dictator named a motorway in the occupied Sahara after ‘Donald Trump’. An occupation of the Sahara that, let us remember, is maintained thanks to the military aid provided by the State of Israel.


The ruling class consciously uses the deliberate scarcity of public resources to pit the working class from one country against that of other territories

. Public services are being privatised, social investment is being cutback – with this money diverted to military spending – and the accumulation of private profits is given primacy, all while it is repeated that the problem lies with those arriving in search of a better life. This discourse has the effect of shifting responsibility away from those who truly concentrate wealth and make economic decisions.


 Migrants are not our enemies. Nor are Moroccan workers, whose exploitation follows the same logic as that suffered by those of us who work in Spain.

Competition does not arise from migration, but from an economic system that requires a precarious workforce

—without rights and easy to exploit—to drive down working conditions as a whole. In this regard, we support regularisation measures that improve living conditions, grant rights and prevent the very competition that the far right so fervently desires.


 As an anarcho-syndicalist organisation,

we reject both Spanish and Moroccan nationalisms. No state represents the interests of the working class.

 In the face of those who use borders to defend geopolitical or economic interests, we call for international solidarity amongst workers.


 The answer cannot be the closure of borders, their militarisation, or international conflict. Neither can we accept that public services remain deliberately underfunded, whilst military spending is increased, according to Trump’s wishes, and a wealthy minority gets even richer.

The only viable solution for the social majority is socialising wealth, guaranteeing adequate public services for all and strengthening the organisation of the working class, regardless of their origin or nationality.

author: Eleanor Morley
title: The problems of AI are the problems of capitalism
content:
Recent revelations about artificial intelligence models “going rogue” have raised serious concerns that the technology could soon cause great damage to human society. Already, the production and application of AI is wreaking havoc on the environment, amplifying existing social problems and expanding the powers of the surveillance state. While further regulation of the industry is necessary, the fundamental problem with AI is that capitalists control it and it is subject to the system’s prevailing conditions of profit maximisation, competition, imperial rivalry and more.

“The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade”, Jacob Coxon, a former researcher at Anthropic and OpenAI, the world’s leading frontier AI model developers, wrote on X in early September. Anthropic’s chief safety researcher Evan Hubinger later responded similarly. “We do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans”, he wrote. “I personally think it is >10 percent within the next decade.”

Amid the myriad other doomsday scenarios the world faces—catastrophic weather and mass extinction events from climate change, the threat of inter-imperialist nuclear war, economic collapse and mass starvation and so on—this latest warning of impending catastrophe could get lost. But it’s worth pausing to think about what exactly has just been said by people working at the frontier of this new technology: it might pose an existential risk to humanity. It’s like an automotive engineer warning that the latest car model has a >10 percent chance of killing everyone on the roads, yet constructing and releasing it anyway.

Some people are understandably sceptical. Outrageous claims have been a key part of the hype machine that has attracted trillions of dollars in investment into leading AI firms and the associated ecosystem of tech companies that provide the chips and memory needed to run the models. “My AI is the biggest and scariest” is another way of saying “my AI is the best to invest in”. There are also debates about the technical capabilities/limitations of various forms of AI, debates about what counts as “intelligence” and whether it is possible to replicate it through binary code, and more. 

But if there is even a tiny possibility that AI could hijack autonomous weapons and rain them down on humanity (something Coxon, in an interview with the

New York Times

, claimed is a potential future scenario), then we should immediately halt the development and deployment of AI models until proper safeguards are in place. Under capitalism, profits always trump human life. We have enough evidence for this in the form of tobacco companies fighting against lung cancer science, DuPont’s knowing deployment of cancerous forever chemicals, the fossil fuel industry’s war on climate science and the very existence of the military-industrial complex. So we certainly should not trust AI titans to regulate themselves, as OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has implored us to do.

The problems with AI

AI doomsday predictions are not new—they have been discussed in tech circles for decades and entered the public domain with the launch of ChatGPT nearly four years ago. But the recent warning cut through in a way others haven’t, partly because it coincides with growing hostility to AI and the companies producing it, and partly because anxieties are rising about the pace of AI’s development. 

The hostility is multifaceted. AI data centres are popping up seemingly everywhere, chewing through energy, guzzling water and emitting a constant, loud hum that is reportedly unbearable for nearby residents. AI slop has degraded online spaces, and deepfakes have created a new dystopian category of sexual harassment. And there are fears about what AI will do to the labour market and the education system—no one is buying Silicon Valley’s techno-optimist line that our labour time will be replaced by leisure time funded by a universal basic income. 

Early AI models now seem almost quaint as we move from general chatbots that could churn out a basic essay or a maid of honour speech to AI agents designed to undertake tasks on our behalf and make their own decisions about how to complete them. Take a recent incident in Australia. An AI assistant, asked by its instructor to bump him to the top of the waitlist for a gym class, hacked the gym’s website and booted someone else off the waitlist entirely.

This was a relatively benign example of AI’s capabilities, though …

author: Julius Gavroche
title: The political topography of anarchism
content:
Olaus Magnus, detail from

Carta Marina

, 1539


On old maps, it is common to see areas populated by mythological creatures, mermaids and Amazons, dragons and unicorns. The beings that inhabit the most remote and unexplored regions – those known or presumed to exist, but which are not yet understood – are depicted in great detail. The accounts of the few travellers who have reached these places are passed on by word of mouth and become distorted as they are retold; they are magnified and exaggerated, until from a narrative—presumed to be more or less reliable—an entire imaginary topography emerges, which serves at the same time to prove the existence of the mythical creatures whose territory it delineates. The circular reasoning is evident.  Dragons exist because they live there, at the edge of the world. This places them on the map. And they live there because they exist and must be somewhere. That is why they can feature in the depiction of the world.


Similarly, in the nineteenth century, with the fantastical excesses of the Middle Ages and the Renaissance now a thing of the past, Victorian explorers – salacot hats on their heads and rifles at the ready – set about methodically filling in the gaps that still remained on the maps. Particularly on the African continent, these blank spaces acted as magnets for the colonial powers, which meticulously mapped out the coastline, yet still knew nothing of what lay inland. This presented a seemingly irresistible invitation to minds imbued with evangelising and imperialist fantasies. After all, as Kipling reminds us, it is the white man’s burden. Something similar occurs in politics too. Most of us grow up virtually as functionally illiterate in this sphere, which is not normally considered necessary for adult education. Generally speaking, the education system and society as a whole take the view that a country’s inhabitants must acquire a body of knowledge that will equip them as future workers and productive members of society, but this does not extend to the civic skills essential for political engagement.


Be that as it may, the fact remains that current democratic models restrict effective participation to a caste of professionals, which means that the rest of the population need only possess a bare inkling of how the system works – just enough to cast a vote in a ballot box and accept that the direct management of their affairs is no longer, if you’ll pardon the redundancy, their concern. But it seems that the tendency to invent what one does not know is a constant feature of human psychology. Just like the monsters on medieval maps, the political landscape is riddled with dark and unknown zones – grey areas of which one usually has only vague notions – from which a fantastical image is constructed that replaces more detailed knowledge and makes the latter seem unnecessary. On the basis of these vague notions, the political landscape is divided up, associating certain elements of the ideological spectrum with distant cardinal points and populating it with the corresponding mythological creatures that inhabit it. Evidently, these beings are not a spontaneous product of the imagination, but are often supplied by interested parties, through channels suited to the level of representation being sought. Cinema, television and, above all, the mainstream media supplant formal political education (in the broadest sense), and disseminate prejudices and preconceived images across a mental map that is intuited rather than drawn. Thus, most people (though not all) know that National Socialism lies somewhere to the right (the east?) of the conservatives, but not exactly why, or what the differences between them are. Similarly, the Marxist left lies to the west, in a zone populated by enemies of private property, although nobody knows how they got there, or why. And the anarchists? That’s where the dragons are…


If our knowledge of, shall we say, conventional political options is generally sketchy and vague, our understanding of those that transcend the conventions of the civic common sense of an era enters the realm of the nebulous. We find ourselves on fertile ground for the mythical. Any notion that goes beyond the parameters accepted as unquestionable in the foundations of the current democratic system is perceived as nonsense, difficult to take on board or even to conceive of as possible. Everyone knows that someone has to be in charge, and if not, things descend into …
