author: Unknown
title: Pour une histoire de l'anti-impérialisme anarchiste
content:
La tradition de lutte contre l'impérialisme est ancienne parmi les anarchistes, elle remonte à l'aube du mouvement, dans les années 1860-1870, et se poursuit aujourd'hui encore. De Cuba à l'Égypte, à l'Irlande, de la Macédoine à la Corée, à l'Algérie et au Maroc, le mouvement anarchiste a payé de son sang son opposition à la domination et au contrôle colonial et impérialiste.


Des anarchistes ont participé à des luttes de libération nationale, mais ils ont toujours affirmé que la destruction de l'oppression nationale et de l'impérialisme doit inclure la destruction du capitalisme et du système étatique et mener à la création d'une communauté humaine sur des bases communistes ou collectivistes. Solidaires de toutes les luttes anti-impérialistes, les anarchistes s'efforcent d'en faire des luttes de libération sociale plutôt que nationale. Des sociétés anticapitalistes et anti-impérialistes qui se fondent sur l'internationalisme et non sur un chauvinisme étroit, où les luttes au centre des Empires soient liées étroitement aux luttes des régions colonisées ou opprimées, et où elles soient contrôlées par les ouvriers et les paysans et reflètent leurs intérêts de classe.


En d'autres termes, nous sommes solidaires des mouvements anti-impérialistes mais nous condamnons ceux qui veulent instrumentaliser ces mouvements pour propager des valeurs réactionnaires (tout comme ceux qui s'opposent à la lutte des femmes pour leurs droits au nom d'une prétendue culture) et nous nous battons contre toute tentative de capitalistes ou de petits bourgeois locaux pour s'approprier ces mouvements. Nous dénonçons la répression des mouvements anti-impérialistes par les États, mais nous dénonçons tout autant le droit des États de décider quelles protestations et quelles luttes sont légitimes. Il n'y a pas de libération si seuls changent le langage ou la couleur de la classe dominante.


Contre le nationalisme


Voilà en quoi nous nous distinguons du courant politique qui domine les mouvements de libération nationale depuis la Deuxième Guerre mondiale, l'idéologie du nationalisme.


Selon cette idéologie, la tâche essentielle de la lutte anti-impérialiste consiste à créer des États-nations indépendants : c'est par l'État que la nation en tant que telle pourra exercer sa volonté générale. Kwame N'krumah, le fer de lance de l'indépendance du Ghana, disait : «

 

"Recherchez premièrement le royaume politique" est devenu le principal slogan du Convention People's Party, car sans l'indépendance politique, aucun de nos projets de développement social et économique ne pourrait être appliqué.

 

»

 [

1

]


Pour atteindre cet objectif, les nationalistes prétendent qu'il faut unir toutes les classes au sein de la nation opprimée contre l'oppresseur impérialiste. Ils affirment que l'expérience commune de l'oppression nationale rend secondaires les différences de classes, ou encore que la notion de classe est un concept importé qui ne s'applique pas dans leur cas.


Les intérêts de classe dissimulés derrière l'idéologie nationaliste sont évidents. Historiquement, ce sont la bourgeoisie et la classe moyenne des nations opprimées qui ont inventé et propagé le nationalisme. C'est une forme d'anti-impérialisme qui souhaite se défaire de l'impérialisme mais conserver le capitalisme, un anti-impérialisme bourgeois qui veut donner à la bourgeoisie locale une nouvelle place, la possibilité d'exploiter la classe ouvrière locale et de développer un capitalisme local.


Notre rôle d'anarchistes face aux nationalistes est donc clair : nous pouvons lutter à leurs côtés pour des réformes et des victoires partielles contre l'impérialisme, mais nous luttons contre leur idéologie étatiste et capitaliste. Nous avons pour rôle de gagner le soutien des masses à notre critique de toute domination, d'éloigner les ouvriers et les paysans du nationalisme et de les gagner à notre programme anarchiste et internationaliste de classe.


Bakounine et la Première Internationale


Le soutien aux mouvements de libération procède directement de l'opposition des anarchistes à toute structure politique hiérarchique et aux inégalités économiques, et de leur projet de confédération internationale librement constituée de communes autonomes et d'associations libres de producteurs libres. Mais l'anarchisme rejette nécessairement les solutions étatiques à l'oppression nationale.


Si on peut désigner un fondateur de l'anarchisme, c'est bien Michel Bakounine (1818-1876). Sa théorie …

After reading Kevin Carson’s Anarchist Notes on the Theory of Money, Credit, and Capital, I was struck by two things:

Where the fuck is reproductive labor in this?

Where the fuck is reproductive labor in this?

Here’s where my thoughts have led me so far. If you’re not familiar with mutual credit, I’ve added a summary at the end you can read first – What IS Mutual Credit?

In Anarchist Notes, Carson quotes Thomas Greco on the proper basis of credit issuance:

“It is crucial that the quantity of the exchange medium be balanced with the flow of goods and services coming into the market, and that it be self-adjusting…. If money is properly issued, there will never be any problem of under-supply or over-supply. The quantity of money will always be just the right amount to purchase the goods and services which it represents…. The proper basis of issue is the transfer of value, as it is being exchanged, from a producer to another (potential) producer.”

And later, on what qualifies a participant to issue credit:

“A participant is qualified to put into circulation an amount of ‘money’ up to the amount of his/her sales over a 2 or 3 month period.”

Both treat market activity — value transfer between producers, sales turnover over a recent window — as the natural anchor for credit issuance. The unit of account is calibrated to the flow of legible exchange. This is sensible as far as it goes, but it leaves two substrates unaccounted for, and both matter.

The ecological. “The transfer of value” treats value as a closed loop between producers, but every transfer is also a draw on ecological systems whose regenerative capacity is finite. Issuing credit against value that depends on irreversibly depleting non-substitutable natural capital is issuing claims against a wealth base that may cease to exist. The proper basis of issue isn’t only transfer of value — it’s transfer of value within the limits of what ecological systems can regenerate. Without that constraint built in, the “self-adjusting” property Greco describes is self-adjusting only with respect to the market, not with respect to the substrate the market depends on. The currency floats free of the conditions that make it possible.

The reproductive. Sales-turnover-based credit qualification builds in a structural bias toward productive labor and against the labor that makes productive labor possible in the first place. Every adult capable of generating sales is the product of decades of reproductive work, such as feeding, teaching, protecting, integrating into community life, that doesn’t itself generate sales but without which there is nothing to sell and no one to sell it. A credit system that calibrates issuance to recent sales volume treats this entire substrate as exogenous, the way classical economics treats the household. author: winter oak
title: Real anarchists expose conspiracies!
content:
by Paul Cudenec, who reads the article

here


I hate to be the bearer of bad news, but you are currently reading the words of a

CONSPIRACY THEORIST

!


Shocking, I know, but it must be true because it has been stated as a concrete fact in the shadowy and spooky world of pseudo-anarchist thought-policing.


An anonymous 2023

article

 on the

Montreal Counter Information

 website declared that I had been “actively propagating far-right conspiracy theories about Jewish bankers and trans people”.


There are two points to note here – firstly, that for these pathetic propagandists a “conspiracy theory” is always “far-right” and secondly that they always make it sound as if criticism such as mine is all about

individuals

 (oh, the poor victims!) rather than, as is really the case, about billion-dollar

businesses

.


The article complained: “While Winter Oak was embroiled in some minor conflict in 2018 for defending Assadists and promoting Syria conspiracies, conspiracism was not the majority content on the site until sometime in 2020, when Cudenec seems to have gone all-in on full-throttle conspiracy mongering”.


I wonder what on earth could have happened in that particular year to have provoked that change in my emphasis?


If the authors of that article happen to be reading this (

maybe as part of their job?)

 I would be interested in their response to my recent article ‘

An A-Z of the modern mega-racket

‘.


In particular I would like to know which insights in that piece count as officially authorised anarchist opinion and which they would condemn as “far-right conspiracy theories”.


It is presumably acceptable to the ideological border patrol that anarchists might express antipathy to exploitative investment, to modern wage-slavery, to repressive laws, to privatisation and to wars.


However, I imagine that I would be considered to have strayed across to the “other side” in my criticism of modern art and culture, of the reign of quantity, of vaccination and of ZIM, the zio-imperialist mafia.


But what about banking, development, education, oligarchy, road-building and the instrumentalisation of xenophobia?


What positions are anarchists “allowed” to hold on these issues before they are regarded as “People Who Are Not Comrades”, as the title of the Montreal article so communistically puts it?


The point I am making is, of course, that these attempts to delimit the scope of anarchist analysis of society are absurd.


Anarchism is the rejection of all power from above, all authority, all exploitation, all assaults on individual and communal freedom.


Any genuine anarchist should therefore be committed to

investigating and exposing

 such authority – I would say “illicit authority”, except for the fact that anarchists regard

all

 authority as illicit.


They should be trying to lift the lid on every kind of repressive institution and infrastructure, particularly those which have been carefully hidden from public view and ringed with taboos to frighten away anyone who does not fancy being publicly denounced by the witch-finders.


The deeper you go, the better, if you are

really

 interested in getting to grips with the roots and nature of the system that rules our world and denies us the co-operative and decentralised freedom that anarchism calls for.


But in the mental prison within which certain interests would like to confine anarchist thinking, alarm bells go off once you start approaching issues that have been declared to be out of bounds.


Identifying, challenging and defying these blocks on our understanding and criticism – and indeed seeking to find out how and by whom they have been introduced into the supposedly free-thinking anarchist scene – should also be part of an authentic anarchist’s ongoing journey of discovery.


In other words, the anarchists who are

not really anarchists

 are those who lack the courage and integrity to push on past all the barriers that are placed in their way to prevent them from having a full grasp of what the system is and how it works.


A real anarchist

has to be

 a kind of conspiracy theorist, because power and authority are themselves a conspiracy.


Exposing power and challenging it are

not

 two different and conflicting tasks – conspiracy theorism

versus

 anarchism – but two aspects of one and the same rebellious role.


This truth even (or rather

especially

!) applies to the kind of “conspiracy theory” that provokes the most hysterical …

author: Trojka
title: Relacja z Konferencji anarchistycznej w Manchester ASN9
content:
W dniach 26-28 sierpnia Anarchist Studies Network zorganizowało 9. edycję konferencji, której tematem przewodnim w tym roku było poszukiwanie anarchizmu nie popadającego w antropocentryzm.


Z jednej strony coraz pilniejsze wydaje się uwzględnienie w aktywizmie ochrony środowiska, zwierząt, lasów, czy nawet konkretnych przestrzeni przed eksploatacją i wyniszczeniem dla zysku. Z drugiej strony w kontekście technologii podnoszone są coraz częstsze głosy krytyczne. W głośnej książce Karen Hao przekonuje, że kontrolowany przez korporację rozwój AI ma charakter imperialny, Yanis Varoufakis od lat przestrzega przed koncentracją władzy w rękach technofeudalnych gigantów w rodzaju Amazona, Shoshana Zuboff opisywała proces nasilenia inwigilacji, a na polskim gruncie niedawno Jarosław Urbański pisał o akceleracjonizmie oraz nadmiernych nadziejach pokładanych w nowych technologiach 1 Konferencja skoncentrowana była na przedstawieniu perspektyw ekologicznych, wegańskich i postkolonialnych, refleksji nad możliwością solidarności z  innymi gatunkami czy walką o środowisko. Podnoszone były również kwestie powiązań ludzi z technologią – czy da się obecnie szerzyć anarchistyczne postawy w świecie cyfrowym, coraz bardziej regulowanym przez korporacje? To uwikłanie człowieka w otoczenie, zarówno naturalne jak i techniczne, skłoniło organizatorów do nazwania ostatniej


edycji: More Than Human Anarchism. Konferencja obejmowała nie tylko kilkadziesiąt wykładów pogrupowanych tematycznie, ale również warsztaty wprowadzające, pokazy filmowe, panele dyskusyjne czy stoiska z zinami i książkami m.in. Freedom Press 2 . Motyw przewodni nadawał spójności konferencji, ale jej nie ograniczał, pozostawało wiele przestrzeni na wystąpienia ogółem odnoszące się do historii anarchizmu, kooperatyw, syndykalizmu czy pomocy wzajemnej.


W konferencji wzięli udział badacze akademiccy i aktywiści z całego świata.

Wśród prelegentów znalazł się chociażby Toru Oda – japoński tłumacz „Więziennych wspomnień anarchisty” Alexandra Berkmana czy „Pomocy wzajemnej jako czynnika rozwoju” Piotra Kropotkina. Opowiadał o historii japońskiej recepcji i tłumaczeń książek anarchistycznego księcia. Laurence Davis przedstawił wywrotową wyobraźnię Ursuli Le Guin, jej krytykę wizji linearnego postępu, który łatwo może przerodzić się w kolonizację, zagarnianie


kolejnych zasobów i przestrzeni w imię „cywilizowania”. Wiele referatów przybliżało myśli autorów klasycznych, takich jak Bakunin czy Kropotkin, a niektórzy znajdowali nieoczywiste połączenia, np. poglądów Maxa Stirnera z posthumanizmem Donny Haraway jak w przypadku referatu Elke Van dermijnsbrugge. Tematy toczonych na konferencji dyskusji obejmowały zagadnienia takie jak nowe technologie, zagrożenia związane ze ślepym dążeniem do zwiększania wydajności, traktowanie społeczeństwa jako maszyny – o tym mówili w ramach swojego wystąpienia Nishikant Sheorey i Karn Bianco. 2


 


Przyleciałem do Manchesteru z referatem poświęconym Piotrowi Kropotkinowi, a w szczególności znaczeniu jego wspomnień spisanych w tekście In Russian and French Prisons. Myśl Kropotkina wciąż wydaje się aktualna,


krytykowany przez niego darwinizm społeczny Herberta Spencera dziś nawiedza nas pod postacią neoliberalnej pog

ardy dla

„przegranych” na rynku (survival of the fittest) i postępującej prywatyzacji, a refleksje

Kropotkin

a nad funkcjonowaniem systemu penitencjarnego zdradzają, że te instytucje

utrwalają tylko dyscyplinę oraz pomagają łamać strajki 3 , a nie mogą zapewnić realnego

progresu społecznego. Referat treścią był zbliżony do mojej książk

i Społeczeństwo wobec

państwa wydanej przez Bractwo Trojka.


Konferencja Anarchist Studies Network była okazją do wymienienia się głosów z różnych środowisk, tych aktywistycznych, jak i akademickich. Te rozmowy na różnych poziomach, dotyczące kwestii praktycznych (np. jak organizować akcje bezpośrednie używając cyfrowych narzędzi) i teoretycznych (historia ruchu, analizy przedstawianych w literaturze anarchistycznych utopii) świadczyły o żywotności idei anarchistycznych. Odczuwalna jest potrzeba na wielu polach zdecentralizowanych, horyzontalnych, spontanicznych i bezpośrednich działań, wbrew unifikującym nacjonalistycznym czy militarystycznym


narracjom.

author: Yeryüzü Postası
title: Anarşist Komünistler – Federazione dei Comunisti Anarchici
content:
İtalya merkezli anarşist komünist örgüt Federazione dei Comunisti Anarchici (Anarşist Komünistlerler Federasyonu) tarafından 2003 yılında kaleme alınan “Anarchist Communists: A Question of Class” yazısının Türkçe çevirisini paylaşıyoruz.

Anarşist Komünistler Federasyonu (FdCA), üyelerinin teorik ve stratejik birliği ilkesi üzerine 1985’te kuruldu; bu ilkeye hâlâ bağlıdır ve bağlı kalmaya devam edecektir. Bu ilke, FdCA’nın, tüm federe üyelik tarafından paylaşılan ortak noktalara dayandığı anlamına gelir.

Bu noktalar, Federasyon’un ve politikalarının birliğini temsil eden bir dizi özgün Teorik Belge‘de ortaya konur. Ayrıca, tek bir politik örgütlenme içinde federe olmuş ve FdCA’nın politik yaşamından ve politik kararlarından bireysel ve kolektif olarak sorumlu olan militanlarının birliğini de temsil eder.

Teorik Belgelerimiz Teori, Temel Strateji, Politik Strateji ve Genel Taktikler olarak bölünmüştür.

Teorimizi oluşturan belgeler, Federasyon’un özgün, birleşik ve karakteristik kimliğini temsil eder. Federasyon’un devrimci rolünü ve tarihsel bellek ve etkin azınlık olarak politik işlevini ortaya koyarlar; bu rol, sınıf mücadelesi tarihi boyunca devrimci proletaryanın deneyimi tarafından işaret edilmiştir.

Teorimiz şu anda iki ana belgeden oluşur: “Teoria dei Comunisti Anarchici” ve “Comunisti Anarchici: Una questione di classe.” Bu broşür, bu ikinci belgenin, ilk olarak 2003’te yayınlanan bir çevirisidir.

Temel Strateji, sınıf düşmanlarımızın uzun vadeli stratejik rolünü, kitle örgütlenmesinin ve politik örgütlenmenin rolünü ve bu örgütlenmelerin komünizme geçiş sırasındaki görevlerini ortaya koyan belgelerden oluşur. Politik Strateji, sınıf mücadelesinin toplumsal, politik ve ekonomik bağlamını ve kitle örgütlenmelerinin ve politik örgütlenmenin stratejik rolünü kısa vadede ortaya koyan belgelerden oluşurken, Genel Taktiklerimiz bu örgütlenmelerin sınıf mücadelesinin mevcut bağlamı içindeki acil rolüyle ilgilenir.

Bu Teorik Belgeler sistemi, FdCA’nın her zaman kendi rolünün ve eylemlerinin doğasını anlayabilecek bir konumda olması ve sürekli bir stratejik düşünüm ve analiz süreciyle meşgul olabilmesi, her zaman sınıf mücadelesinden öğrenmesi, iç tartışmayı teşvik etmesi ve böylece ideolojik katılıktan kaçınması için tasarlanmıştır.

www.fdca.it web sitemizde, Teorik Belgelerimizin çoğunu İtalyanca olarak ve Temel Strateji ile Genel Taktiklere dair çeşitli belgeleri de İngilizce olarak bulabilirsiniz.

Federazione dei Comunisti Anarchici Uluslararası İlişkiler Ofisi Haziran 2005

Anarşist Komünizm, entelektüel bir maceranın saf meyvesi değildir. Ne kadar mutlu olursa olsun, tarihten korunmuş, insanlığın kaderi üzerine düşünen belirli bireylerin bir sonucu değildir. Çağdaş toplumun kötülüklerine ve apaçık adaletsizliklerine karşı birkaç ütopyacının (cömert) yanıtı değildir. Soyut düşünmeye ihtiyaç duyan zihinlerin uyum ihtiyacını karşılayabilecek bir mükemmellik idealinin arayışı değildir. Anarşist Komünizm, hem proletaryanın mücadelesinden hem de bu mücadelelerin bizzat içinden doğmuştur ve bu yüzden, insanın daha az adaletsiz toplumsal örgütlenme biçimlerine yönelik doğuştan gelen özlemleriyle pek az ilgisi vardır. Bu yüzden, köklerini az çok eski zamanların felsefi sistemlerinde aramayacağız (bunlar, aynı zamanda ortaya çıkan diğer bazı politik düşünce biçimlerinde, Marksizm ya da liberal ideoloji gibi, olduğu gibi düşüncemiz için besin sağlamış olsa da). Yalnızca, İşçi ve Proleter hareketinin bir bileşeninde, Birinci Enternasyonal’den (1864) başlayıp bugüne kadar süren fikirlerin katmanlaşmasına odaklanacağız.

Tüm bunlar, ancak, Anarşist Komünizm adını taşıyan ideolojik bütünün gelişimine temel bir katkı sağlayan düşünümlere sahip bireylerin hiç olmadığı anlamına gelmez ve onları üç öncülle birlikte kısa bölümler ile ayıracağız. Birincisi, hiçbirinin, sınıf mücadelesindeki olayların evrimini dışarıdan gözlemleyen ya da yönlendirici bir role sahip olan, ona yalnızca politikalar ve analizler sağlama görevi veren salt bir düşünür olmadığıdır. Hepsi, hareketin gündelik işleyişinde tam zamanlı olarak politik olarak katılan ve bu nedenle katkıları sık sık bütünlüklü değildir, anın sıcaklığında aceleyle yazılmış, düşünce çizgisi devam eden ve çoğunlukla bir sonuca ulaştırılmamış tek seferlik makalelerden ya da broşürlerden oluşur. author: Nada Elia
title: Women and Youth Are at the Forefront of the Struggle for Palestinian Liberation
content:
They follow in the footsteps of Palestinian women and children who have resisted colonialism in the past century.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

I grew up in a household of women and children that, as my sisters and I matured, eventually became a household of only women. My father was frequently gone on long overseas business trips before his untimely death when I was seven. I often wonder if this is the reason the expression “women and children” strikes me as essentially flawed: It suggests that women and children are the more vulnerable members of society, rather than its resilient survivors. It infantilizes women by grouping them with children, rather than adult men.

In the context of a national struggle, it strips women of agency, as if such agency can only manifest through armed revolt. In a military context, the expression “women and children” — or “womenandchildren,” to use the term coined by antimilitary feminist scholar Cynthia Enloe — presumes that women and children never take up arms or participate in resistance, even as we see such actions occurring in numerous struggles around the world. And in listing casualties, it implies that men’s deaths and injuries are less tragic, less mournable.

In the case of Palestine, women and youth have led, and continue to lead, some of the most transformative efforts and initiatives in our people’s quest for justice — that is, our resistance first to imperialism, then to settler colonialism and apartheid. They have not been spared Israel’s violence, just for being women, or children, and many have been and remain at the forefront of popular resistance to Zionism’s ultimate aim of eliminating all Palestinians. While this may have become more obvious during Israel’s accelerated genocidal assault on Gaza following Hamas’s October 7, 2023, attacks, it had always been clear to anyone not deliberately looking away.

From a number of uprisings over the past century in Palestine, it is obvious that youth, “the children,” are not just among the leaders; they are the more effective, more transformational leaders. Unfettered by traditions and social norms they do not relate to, they engage in novel forms of organizing, seeking the complete abolition of oppressive systems, rather than their reversal. And women, in their capacity as autonomous adults, rather than merely as wives and mothers, have consistently resisted both the imperial ideology targeting their country, and the military assaults that accompanied it. They did so while providing men, as well as the youth and children, the moral, emotional, and practical support the Palestinian people need in order to persist. This was perhaps most evident on a global scale during the 1987–93 Intifada, when women organized most of the popular committees tending to the educational, nutritional, and health needs of Palestinians resisting Israel’s clampdown, as youth took to the streets daily to express their rejection of Israel’s decades-long oppressive rule. These defenseless children hurled rocks at armored tanks, fully aware of the hefty price they would pay for their defiant act, because they knew that risking limb and life is preferable to living without freedom and dignity.

Women’s and children’s agency is enacted daily in the courage of girls such as Janna Jihad, who was dubbed “the world’s youngest journalist” when she started documenting Israel’s crimes at a mere seven years of age. Jihad started recording Israel’s attacks using her mother’s cell phone, posting her recordings far and wide on social media. She has repeatedly said that her camera is her weapon of choice. Jihad is the cousin of Ahed Tamimi, the “lioness” who has confronted heavily armed Israeli soldiers determined to take over her village lands since she was a toddler. Israel imprisoned Tamimi for eight months when she was sixteen; she used the time behind bars to read up on international law, later enrolling in college planning to go to law school, so as to hold Israel accountable for its violations. “I am a freedom fighter. So I will not be the victim,” she told journalists upon her release.

Palestinian children’s agency was also clear in the 2022 uprising of rebellious youth standing up to Israel’s might. Ibrahim al-Nabulsi, dubbed “the Lion of Nablus,” was eighteen when he was brutally assassinated by the Israeli Occupation Forces. Following his martyrdom, his mother, Huda al-Nabulsi …

author: ROAPE
title: Food security or seed capture? The colonial potato and Africa’s seed wars
content:
It all begins with a potato. Not the kind that nourishes a nation in textbook stories, but a colonial potato. This potato was shipped, tested, rationed, pushed through mission gardens and military supply lines, and ultimately sold as progress. Tracing that potato across Nigeria’s highlands leads to today’s disputes over seed, debt, law, and who decides what African farmers cultivate. 


Seeds are not just seeds. They carry memory, labour, taste, law, power, and often, debt.

The colonial potato scheme in Nigeria

 is significant because it shows how dependency on seeds can develop even before it is codified in law. Nowadays, discussions about seed sovereignty in Africa often centre on patents, plant breeders’ rights, certified seed laws, and agribusiness. However, colonial Nigeria reveals an older method of control: emergency.       


In the 1930s and 1940s, British officials transformed the

Jos and Mambila Plateaus

 into experimental sites for growing potatos. Initially, the scheme was small and awkward, driven by European miners, missionaries, and colonial officers seeking familiar food. Then, the Second World War (1939-1945) changed everything. Supply routes were disrupted, troops needed food, and Nigerian highland farmers were forcibly integrated into a larger imperial food plan. An agricultural experiment became part of the British empire’s war effort.


An anthropological base map of Plateau Province reproduced from C.G. Ames, The Gazetteers of Plateau Province, 1932 (Copy in Nigerian National Archives, Kaduna)


The highlands were ideal for the crop. Potatos thrive in cooler conditions, and Jos and Mambila provided the climate colonial agronomists desired. However, these areas were not empty spaces waiting for improvement. They were inhabited, farmed, and politically complex societies with their own crops, markets, and knowledge systems.


Colonial rule altered the dynamics in these regions. Tin mining on the Jos Plateau attracted workers, administrators, and settlers. Demand for European foods increased. Potatos, once a garden crop for expatriates and mission stations, began to seem valuable to the colonial state.


Starting in the 1930s, British

officials based in Nigeria began importing seed potatos from Ireland, Britain, Europe, South Africa, the Canary Islands, and the United States.

 Mission stations cultivated the potatos. District heads distributed the seed. Farmers cautiously tried the crop, incorporating it into local routines where it made sense while rejecting it when it didn’t. The potato became a means of power.


This did not mean that older crops and seed systems disappeared. There was no formal ban, and local farmers continued to grow, save, and exchange seed in various ways. The scheme worked in subtler ways: it altered the rewards. Access to land, labour, credit, official support, and markets began to favour the colonial crop. Imported seed was seen as improved, while farmer-saved seed and local knowledge were pushed to the sidelines. Over time, diverse and adaptable seed systems were narrowed, though not completely erased, by a supply chain prioritising mines, mission stations, military demands, and imperial markets.


Before the Second World War, the scheme was no great success. Some farmers thought potatos were poisonous. Others saw no reason to cultivate a crop with a limited, European-dominated market. A 1937 attempt to sell imported ‘Great Scott’ seed potatos to the Jos Native Authority ended poorly: half went unsold, the remainder was given away, and the scheme lost money.


War transformed failure into urgency. The empire needed food close to military outposts. It aimed to save cargo space and lessen reliance on disrupted shipping routes. Suddenly, potatos on the Mambila and Jos Plateau became crucial.


The war economy and the creation of dependency


Production surged from around

90 tons at the beginning of the war in 1939 to about 1,200 tons by 1943. Seed stores and experimental stations emerged throughout Kagoro, Zonkwa, Kurmin Biri, and Riyom

. Colonial science advanced rapidly, too: London-based Kew scientists devised ways to transport sprouting ‘eyes’ of potatos instead of whole tubers, facilitating a steady supply from outside.


Wartime officials did not establish an independent Nigerian seed system; they created a supply chain. Farmers were encouraged to boost production. Yet, this authority remained elsewhere: seed, disease control, imports, and markets remained …

author: Pip Hinman
title: Ecosocialism 2026 forges unity and builds struggles
content:
“The big people behind capitalism are quite aware that they are planning the end of the world as we know it”, Sabrina Fernandes, a political economist and ecosocialist activist from Brazil, told the Ecosocialism 2026 conference in Magan-djin/Brisbane, September 11–13.

“They don’t have a problem with the world ending as we know it — as long as they can keep making profits,” Fernandes said.

“They do have a problem with a society that they might not be able to control when things get really hard, as we are coming to this stage of ecocide and global catastrophe. They are fighting over the spoils of war and climate change.”

Places that would not normally be considered part of the grab are becoming so, Fernandes said. The oceans “are a new terra nullius for them” — for ocean floor mining.

There should be an international agreement for this, but US President Donald Trump does not care and has begun issuing his own licences, she added.

Helen Yaffe, author, activist and Professor of Latin American Political Economy, University of Glasgow, told the conference that socialist Cuba, one of the key targets of Trump’s new colonialism, is facing multiple and mounting challenges as the US blockade intensifies.

The response that she has witnessed, in a recent visit to Cuba, was: “We shall not submit!”

“Revolutionary Cuba wrote the rulebook on resilience,” Yaffe said. Facing a total oil blockade since January, Cuba is now undertaking an incredibly rapid transition to renewable energies.

“Many commentators are saying this will be the fastest ever transition.” Solar panel parks now supply more than 60% of electricity on some days, but Yaffe said the challenge is storage.

Singaporean ecosocialist See Yong Feng, another guest speaker, told Green Left that capitalism is holding back human development.

“The need for limitless economic growth is often framed as the only way to solve global poverty, but new research strongly disproves this. The world already uses way more than enough energy and materials to provide a decent standard of living for all, but the profit-driven capitalist system prevents this from happening.

“We can both address poverty and the climate crisis, as long as we break the capitalist elites’ control of our economy and democratise our production and consumption,” See said.

The Gaza genocide, Trump’s blatant disregard for international and domestic laws and his naked colonial violence symbolise the ugly reality that is forging a new generation of activists, Alex Bainbridge, a conference organiser, told GL.

“Trump has his admirers and imitators all around the world, including Marine Le Pen in France, Narendra Modi in India and Pauline Hanson here.

“But while far-right politicians push hard, there is a sharp reaction and a growing resistance; this conference was a powerful reminder of that,” Bainbridge said.

Remah Naji, a leading activist with Justice for Palestine Magan-djin, expressed this resistance. “Maybe we can’t stop a fascist and psychopath like Netanyahu from committing the war crimes he’s committing … but I can hold my government to account.”

The conference included a solidarity concert with Phil Monsour and an art exhibition.

Markela Panegyres, another conference organiser and curator of the art exhibition, told GL: “From the ongoing genocide in Gaza, to the endless drive to more wars and militarism, to ecocide, to the rise of the far right, the depravity of US-led imperialism and global capitalism is reaching ever-higher levels.

“The gravity of this moment demands that art and artists play an active role in resistance.

“This is why the concept of cultural intifada is so important: Art should not be merely a reflection of life, or entertainment or a commodity, but a weapon in the struggle for our collective liberation.

“The work of the artists, musicians and theatre makers who participated in the cultural intifada round-table and exhibition demonstrated the importance of art in movement-building.

“We were so proud that Aunty Sue Coleman-Haseldine, a senior Googatha Elder, Maralinga survivor and long-term anti-nuclear activist, came all the way from the Googatha Nation in the west of South Australia, north of Ceduna.”

Coleman-Haseldine talked about the campaign against rocket and weapons testing on her Country and her opposition to AUKUS and to US military and surveillance bases.

Ecosocialism 2026 was sponsored by the Socialist Alliance, Green Left, Resistance Books and Links — International …

title: “Logic of Elimination” Drives Israel’s Policies in the West Bank, Report Finds
content:
The report says Israel is “dramatically intensifying its attacks on every aspect of Palestinian life in the West Bank.”

A major new report by the Israeli human rights group B’Tselem titled “The Elimination Project” accuses Israel of “dramatically intensifying its attacks on every aspect of Palestinian life in the West Bank.”

“For too long, Israel’s policies in the West Bank have been treated or looked at as isolated events,” says Ori Givati, director of international relations at B’Tselem. “We actually find that there is one very coherent logic behind all of them, and this is the logic of elimination of Palestinian collective life in the West Bank.” Givati says tactics against Palestinians intensified with Israel’s 2022 election and again after October 7, 2023, adding that “we are definitely seeing a lot of the mechanisms, the tools that were used and are used still … in Gaza, being implemented in the West Bank.”

We also speak with Mohammad Sha’ban, a Palestinian farmer from Halhul in the Hebron area of the occupied West Bank who says 11 gates and seven settler outposts have been installed around Halhul since 2025. “We cannot reach our lands. We cannot go outside Halhul. They open only one gate from 8 o’clock until 5 o’clock every day,” says Sha’ban. Settlers “attack farmers, beat farmers … damaging our cars, also damaging our fields, uprooting our trees.”

author: Susan Price
title: Singapore’s unfinished anti-colonial struggle
content:
The dominant history of modern Singapore was meticulously constructed under the banner of the “Singapore Story”. By presenting the material interests of the ruling elite as the universal interests of the nation, the state narrative reduces the mass anti-imperialist movement of the mid-20th century into a fable; one wherein a heroic bourgeois leadership single-handedly navigates a vulnerable island state through the perils of communism to construct a prosperous capitalist metropolis.

In his six-part oral history series with Pintjin (PJ) Thum, Dr Poh Soo Kai, former student activist, co-founder of the People’s Action Party (PAP) and the Barisan Sosialis (Socialist Front) — and former political prisoner detained for nearly 17 years without trial — delivers a vital historical materialist counter-narrative.

In 36 minutes of personal testimony, Poh unpacks the class dynamics, state coercion, and geopolitical shake-ups that dismantled working-class power and shaped Singapore's transition into a disciplined capitalist state.

Poh begins by recalling how post-World War II Malayan households were adorned with portraits of Indonesia’s Sukarno, India’s Nehru and Gandhi, and China’s Chiang Kai-Shek, who were seen as regional anti-colonial leaders. The struggle in Singapore was bound to broader anti-imperialist movements across Malaya, Indonesia, and Vietnam.

Poh’s account of the 1954 Fajar Trial undermines the state’s origin myth, which positions the trial of eight members of the editorial board of Fajar (Dawn) — the University of Malaya Socialist Club’s newspaper — as Lee Kuan Yew’s (LKY’s) personal legal breakthrough.

[Editor’s note: Harry Lee Kwan Yew co-founded the PAP, was a barrister and opposition figure and became Singapore’s first Prime Minister in 1959.]

As president of the University of Malaya Socialist Club, Poh helped publish Fajar, an anti-colonial paper opposing the anti-communist South East Asian Treaty Organisation (SEATO) and foreign military bases. When the editorial board was charged with sedition, Queen’s Counsel DN Pritt arrived to lead the defense. Poh recounts Pritt greeting him warmly at the Dolphin Hotel before turning to LKY, who was acting as local junior counsel, and saying, “Harry, now you can go.”

Pritt dismissed LKY specifically to formulate an anti-colonial strategy directly with the student activists, recognising that the trial was a political battlefield rather than a legal technicality.

This moment symbolises the clash between the radical student movement and LKY’s legalism, and how official history later repackaged a left-wing victory as an LKY solo masterstroke.

As the PAP rose to power, internal contradictions between its left-wing mass base and moderate leadership erupted.

Poh recounts how the left wing consistently pushed for true self-determination, confronting PAP Chair Toh Chin Chye to issue a public statement supporting then-Chief Minister David Marshall’s 1956 call for internal self-rule — a move that infuriated LKY upon his return from London.

[Editor’s note: Marshall was appointed Chief Minister after contesting the 1955 election as a candidate for the Labour Front. After failing to secure self-rule, he resigned as Chief Minister in June 1956.]

Chief Minister Lim Yew Hock’s violent crackdowns on trade unions and Chinese school students from 1956 onward served a dual purpose: suppressing working-class organisation while allowing LKY to position himself as the sensible alternative acceptable to British imperial interests and local capital.

When dissident MPs and activists walked out to form the Barisan Sosialis in 1961, every PAP branch including LKY’s own Tanjong Pagar constituency defected to the new party. The PAP was left as a hollow electoral vessel without organic mass support.

To preempt an electoral defeat, the state deployed Operation Coldstore in February 1963. Officially framed as a security operation against a communist plot tied to the 1962 Brunei Revolt, Coldstore was a draconian political purge that sought to decapitate the political opposition, dismantle union leadership and ensure PAP hegemony.

The state weaponised identity politics to divide the multi-ethnic working-class by branding Chinese-educated labour leaders and Barisan Sosialis members as “Chinese chauvinists”. It replaced class-based solidarity with state-directed multiracialism that contained labour organising within non-threatening boundaries.

author: Ruby Healer
title: Labor doubles down on US military alliance
content:
“American force posture in Australia is growing”, Australian Defence Minister Richard Marles declared on his visit to Washington, DC, this month. “Since we’ve come to government”, Marles said, standing alongside US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, “you can see a through line there of growing American force posture in Australia”.

It was a fairly straightforward summary of the Albanese Labor government’s attitude, followed up with promises of further integration between the Australian and US militaries. A shifting “force posture” will mean more American troop rotations, more US air and naval operations and more pre-positioning of military equipment like warplanes, fuel and munitions in Australia.

Agreements made by the Albanese government will ramp up co-operation on all fronts, with a newly

revitalised

 HMAS Stirling base near Perth set to host American nuclear-powered submarines and an estimated 2,300 US troops within five years. As America’s military machine looks ahead to an era of aggressive contest with China in the Asia-Pacific, Australia’s ruling class is desperate to make itself an indispensable part of US war planning.

Weapons trade regulations have also been

loosened

 under a bilateral agreement to help both countries access shared research to develop arms and surveillance systems. And, Marles promised ominously, “you will hear more from us ... in the coming months” about further arrangements to increase co-operation.

Of course, there’s nothing new about the Australian ruling class throwing itself into a military alliance with the United States. This is a long-standing arrangement pursued by every Australian government since the Second World War. Permanent joint intelligence and communications programs have run out of Pine Gap in the Northern Territory and the Harold Holt naval station in Western Australia since the 1960s.

Data

published

 by the

Guardian

 in early September revealed that American forces and weapons corporations control or make use of over 100 military facilities across the country. And Australia is one of the biggest recipients of US arms in the world, with around 85 percent of weapons purchased in 2021-25 coming from the US,

according

 to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute’s arms transfers database.

Hegseth himself

recalled

 during a separate love-in event with Marles last year: “We [the Australian and US militaries] fought shoulder to shoulder in every major conflict since World War One—from the Western Front, to Guadalcanal, to Vietnam, to Afghanistan”.

“During my time in Afghanistan”, he reminisced, “I served with members of the Australian military who were some of the finest”. We can only imagine the sorts of unconvicted war criminals who consorted with Pete Hegseth during the joint twenty-year occupation of Afghanistan.

The US alliance has long been a pillar of Australia’s foreign policy, but the current Labor government seems particularly eager to grovel to America. Just one month after Donald Trump’s inauguration, and before the current Australian and US defence ministers had even met for the first time, the Australian government arranged a

payment

 of US$500 million towards the Trump administration’s military budget.

“We’re really pleased that the first payment ... we’ve been able to make in the first couple of weeks of the Trump administration”, Marles told Hegseth ahead of their first formal meeting in February 2025. “We’re really pleased to make it in the first week of your tenure as the secretary of defence.”

In the meeting that followed, Marles

explained

 that Hegseth’s enthusiasm for military ties with Australia made sense, since “the whole idea of a free and open Indo-Pacific really has its origins during the first Trump Administration”.

You wouldn’t be wrong to interpret this behaviour as pathetic bootlicking. The Australian government is a simpering bunch of pro-American lowlifes. But the problem isn’t that our leaders are “weak” or being strong-armed into subservience. They run the twelfth largest economy in the world. Their armed forces outstrip those of any oceanic neighbours by a wide margin. The reality is that Australian capitalism is a willing and culpable participant in the world’s most powerful military coalition alongside America.

As former Labor Prime Minister Kevin Rudd recently

stated

, the “alliance with the United States remains a force multiplier for Australia’s defence needs”. With the help of its powerful …

title: Türkiye-Yunanistan gerilimi: Sadece bir sınır sorunu değil emperyalist planda yer kapma meselesi
content:
Seyit Aldoğan [email protected]

Atina- Son dönemde Ortadoğu, Doğu Akdeniz, Ege ve İran ekseninde gelişen ABD-İsrail savaşının yaygınlaşma eğilimi, bir anlamda Türk-Yunan ilişkilerini de tetikledi. Bu durum Türkiye basınında “Atina’da deprem”, “Atina gerilim istiyor”, “Yunanistan ve İsrail ablukası” benzeri manşetlerin atılmasına neden oldu. Karşılıklı restleşmeler, uyarılar ve milliyetçi söylemlerle düşmanlığı körükleyen değerlendirmeler havada uçuşuyor.

Dünyada emperyalist rekabetin kızışmasına, pazar paylaşımı mücadelesine ve emperyalist savaşların yaygınlaşma eğilimi içine girmesine paralel olarak, üzerinde yaşadığımız coğrafyada da enerji nakil hatları, hidrokarbon rezervleri ve deniz taşımacılığı gibi etkenlere bağlı olarak Türkiye-Yunanistan ilişkilerinde yeni bir gerginliğe doğru gidildiği görülüyor.

ABD ve onun bölgedeki vurucu gücü olan İsrail yeni bir yapılanmayı hedeflerken, bölgedeki gerici yönetimler pastadan pay kapmak, emperyalist sistemin bir parçası olarak varlıklarını sürdürmeyi güvence altına almak ve bölgesel çıkar dengeleri içinde daha iyi bir mevzi tutmak amacıyla dış politika, ticaret, silahlanma ve ittifaklarda yeni yönelimler içine giriyorlar. Bölge gericiliklerinin çıkarlarının farklılıklar göstermesi emperyalizme bağımlılıkla çelişmediği gibi, tersine bu bağımlılığı daha da güçlendiren birer etmen haline geliyor.

Bölgedeki gelişmelere bu perspektifle bakıldığında Türkiye ve Yunanistan arasında anlaşmazlık konusu olan sorunların klasik anlamda bir sınır sorunu olmaktan çıktığı açıkça görülecektir.

Rusya Karadeniz, Balkanlar ve Doğu Avrupa’dan abluka altına alınıyor. Yunan adalarına hava savunma sistemlerinin yerleştirilerek Ege kontrol altına alınmaya çalışılıyor. Doğu Trakya ABD-NATO üssüne çevriliyor. Öte yandan Doğu Akdeniz’de İsrail, Güney Kıbrıs ve Yunanistan arasında enerji nakil anlaşmasının yürürlüğe girmesi, Yunanistan’ın münhasır ekonomik bölge çerçevesi içinde uluslararası tekellerle yaptığı anlaşmalar, enerji rezervlerinin önemi, Ortadoğu’ya müdahalede bölgenin önem kazanması, Çin ve Rusya ile girişilen rekabet vb. gelişmeler Türkiye ile Yunanistan arasındaki sorunların artık klasik anlaşmazlıklar olmaktan çıktığını gösteriyor. Gelişmeler, Ege ve Doğu Akdeniz’i emperyalist yayılmacılık, paylaşım ve egemenlik rekabetinin açıkça görüldüğü alan durumuna getiriyor.

Yunanistan’da 1973 yılında yıkılan Albaylar Cuntası sonrasından bugüne kadar kurulan en işbirlikçi yönetim olan Kiryakos Miçotakis’nin Yeni Demokrasi (ND) hükümeti, Ege’de ve Doğu Akdeniz’de Yunan sermayesinin çıkarları doğrultusunda başta ABD, İsrail ve sonrasında AB ile, son derece stratejik anlaşmalar yapmış bulunuyor. Mısır, Lübnan, BAE, Suudi Arabistan ile askeri ve ticari ve teknik ilişkiler geliştirdi. Bu arada özellikle Fransız ve Alman tekellerinin çıkarlarının sözcülüğünü de yapıyor.

Erdoğan hükümeti ise ABD ve AB destekli İsrail, Yunanistan ve Güney Kıbrıs kesimi eksenine karşı Suriye’de sahip olduğu etkiyi, son süreçte Pakistan ve Suudi Arabistan ile kurulan “Mekke ittifakı”nı, ABD ve NATO politikaları ile tam bir uyum içinde olan tutumunu; Trump’ın övgüsünü kazanan İran ve Filistin politikasını, NATO politikaları çerçevesi içinde artan silahlanma harcamalarını kullanarak elini güçlendirmeye ve bölge ülkeleriyle kurduğu ekseni güçlendirmeye çalışıyor.

Kuşkusuz her iki ülkenin bağımlılığı daha fazla artıran bu tutumlarının ana nedeni sadece Türk-Yunan ilişkileri ve Ege-Doğu Akdeniz gibi sorunlarla açıklanamaz. Esas neden bölgede oluşan ya da oluşması olası olan dengelerden pay kapma yarışıdır. Türkiye’yi asıl kaygılandıran İsrail’in bölgede oyun kurucu duruma gelme planlarıdır. Örneğin “yavru vatan” ilan edilmesine ramak kalan Suriye’de İsrail’in etkisinin artması ve Colani hükümeti ile anlaşma masasına oturulması, Arap ülkeleriyle İbrahim anlaşmalarının imzalanması, Yunanistan’ın AB üyesi olarak Türkiye ile bölgesel çıkarlar üzerinden iş birliği yapan ülkeler ve tekellerle ekonomik, askeri ve ticari ilişkiler geliştirmesi Türkiye’nin yayılmacı politikaları önünde ciddi engeller oluşturuyor.

Son süreçte ise Yunanistan, Kıbrıs ve İsrail arasında çekilen elektrik hattı ve Türkiye tarafından hazırlanan “Mavi vatan” kanunu ve “deniz parkları” kararı, iki ülke arasında gerginliğin yeniden yükselmesine neden oldu. Yunan hükümeti “Mavi vatan” kanununun “hiçbir geçerliliğinin olmayacağını” savunurken, Dışişleri Bakanı Yorgos Gerapetritis defalarca “Yunanistan her türlü tahrike karşı koymaya hazırdır” …

author: Sarah Raymundo
title: Blood Rush | $100 barrel, super El Niño and Pax Silica: Energy hegemony, enclosure, and national liberation
content:
The AI-assisted illustration of the proposed 1,600-hectare industrial hub to be located in New Clark City in Capas, Tarlac. Photo courtesy of the People’s Television Network

The convergence of crude oil surpassing $100 per barrel and the acceleration of El Niño to “super” status—drawn from projections and reports by energy-market analysts, international economic-monitoring bodies, and climate agencies tracking compound global shocks—exposes the deep structural crisis of monopoly capitalism. This dual rupture demonstrates how imperialist war-making, extractive plunder, planetary warming, and the ongoing enclosure of the countryside function not as separate phenomena, but as interconnected expressions of the same underlying logic of capital accumulation.

The rapid climb of crude oil past $100 per barrel cannot be detached from the escalation of U.S.-led imperialist aggression, military blockades, and regional destabilization. Financialized markets and transnational fossil-fuel monopolies exploit war and artificial scarcity to protect superprofits, while the resulting inflation functions as a mechanism of structural extraction from working classes in colonies and semicolonies. Peripheral societies are forced to absorb the crisis through debt traps, budget cuts, declining purchasing power, and reduced national sovereignty. High energy prices further incentivize ruling elites to expand speculative and destructive extraction projects in the name of energy security and geopolitical hegemony.

This energy regime is increasingly bound up with “Pax Silica”—the global alliance centered on microelectronics, semiconductor supply chains, and automated defense systems. Localized military interventions rely on a global network of critical mineral extraction, energy consumption, and defense technology transfer. The fusion of high-tech militarism and fossil capital reinforces imperialist control over global supply lines, shifting the operational costs of planetary warfare directly onto the working classes of the Global South.

At the same time, a “super” El Niño brings the violence of ecological crisis directly to the doorsteps of the global peasantry, smallholders, and urban poor. Although the historical carbon footprint belongs overwhelmingly to the industrial centers of the imperialist world, the physical destruction—manifested in crop failures, severe drought, flooding, and damaged infrastructure—falls disproportionately on semicolonial societies. Framing these events as merely “natural disasters” shields the capitalist mode of production from critique and obscures climate catastrophe as an institutionalized assault on oppressed and economically vulnerable populations.

Far from resolving the agrarian question, this ecological and economic squeeze accelerates what Paris Yeros calls generalized semiproletarianization. In this condition, households that have lost all or part of their means of production do not become fully dependent on wages. Instead, they combine precarious employment with small-scale farming, petty trade, subsistence production, care work, and other sources of livelihood (Yeros, 2023). Across much of the Global South, this blurs the conventional boundary between peasant and worker and produces socially fragmented labor forces that move between rural and urban economies (Moyo & Yeros, 2005; Moyo et al., 2013; Yeros, 2024).

Under conditions of monopoly capitalism, these labor reserves can weaken workers’ bargaining power and shift the costs of social reproduction onto households and communities (Marx, 1976; Yeros, 2023). Millions may circulate between degraded smallholder farming, informal street trade, temporary migration, and precarious wage work without being absorbed into secure urban industrial employment. Rather than representing a simple transition from peasant production to wage labor, semiproletarianization describes a durable social formation in which rural and urban livelihood strategies remain interdependent (Yeros, 2023).

To propose “ecosocialism” as a generic, off-the-shelf alternative to this twin crisis, without subjecting the term itself to critical scrutiny, is to risk reproducing a dangerous conceptual trap. Much dominant Western-centered ecosocialist discourse reduces the problem to an abstract, planet-wide carbon-accounting exercise. In doing so, it can erase the national question, gloss over the unresolved agrarian question, and ignore the necessity of national-liberation struggles in …

author: Pip Hinman
title: Big data and the AUKUS war machine
content:
The world’s greatest remilitarisation since the World War II is underway, driven by the imperatives of the flailing United States empire.

The AUKUS war pact places us at the centre of this drive towards war. How should we imagine Australia’s role in the world?

Australia is not just a settler-colonial state; it is a sub-imperial power that has transferred subordination from its one-time colonial ruler, Britain, to the US, its new imperial master.

It is now acting to preserve the military and economic interests of its master state. This is encapsulated in the AUKUS war pact, which, despite no public debate, commits the country to eight nuclear-powered submarines, high-tech weapons development and sharing and the subsequent invasion of US personnel and weaponry in the event of our “interoperability” in a contrived future conflict with China.

Through AUKUS, Australia acts as a mechanism for US force projection into the Pacific, to rattle the sabre against China.

AUKUS makes Australia the first non-nuclear-weapons state to use a loophole in the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons for naval propulsion with weapons-grade uranium.

That sets a proliferation precedent.

Climate change is the real security threat. Pacific leaders named climate change their main security threat in the 2018 Boe Declaration. Yet Australia keeps expanding fossil fuel exports while spending hundreds of billions on submarines.

But AUKUS is about so much more than submarines; its more sinister part is AUKUS Pillar II, which is about “advanced capabilities” including: undersea capabilities; quantum science; artificial intelligence (AI) and autonomy; advanced cyber; hypersonics and counter-hypersonics; and electronic warfare.

Any pretense about “defensive” capabilities is put to rest with Pillar II because these technologies are about highly efficient offensive war-fighting capabilities.

The Australian Human Rights Commission said it is arguably impossible for AI to comply with the proportionality rule, because AI is unable to understand the intrinsic value of human life.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres said that machines determining proportionality in life-or-death situations is “politically unacceptable and morally repugnant”.

Australia said in 2018 that it was premature to regulate Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems. Nearly a decade later, it maintains this position despite significant advances and uses of the technology.

It is instead barrelling ahead with developing the most advanced and lethal forms imaginable.

The first “signature project” of AUKUS Pillar II was announced in May — payloads and systems for uncrewed undersea vehicles are due from 2027, covering surveillance, reconnaissance, strike, anti-submarine and electronic warfare, among other missions.

The stated aim is meeting near-term war fighting objectives. The Ghost Shark project for Australia is being developed by Silicon Valley-based defence contractor Anduril. Defence Industry Minister Pat Conroy said they will conduct surveillance and can strike at extremely long distances. It means the weapon is designed to operate far from our shores — not for defence.

Pillar II extends into the realms of software and artificial intelligence. Tests for active warfighting scenarios to integrate Australian, British and US AI models have been ongoing for years.

A 2023 pilot had Australia PA-8 Poseidon aircraft sharing data for submarine detection, amid other tests of “AI-enabled assets” and machine-learning models.

There was a large-scale US trial in 2024. The US Department of War was enthusiastic: “These trials demonstrated significant progress since the first AUKUS RAAIT trails in the UK in April 2023 and show tangible results of the AUKUS Pillar II commitment to making our warfighter more lethal on the battlefield.

“It used to be that each nation used its own datasets to develop separate models and deploy those models on their own platforms. Under RAAIT, we’ve matured the AI pipeline, focusing on interchangeability and interoperability, which allows for any combinations of datasets, models, algorithms and platforms to be used across all three nations.”

These models and cloud computational capacity are key to war power investments today.

The Pentagon’s AI office awarded Anthropic, Google, OpenAI and xAI contracts worth up to US$200 million each for military and intelligence AI last year.

author: Unknown
title: Emon Azmi - Solidarity has to have teeth
content:
Author

: Emon Azmi

Title

: Solidarity has to have teeth

Subtitle

: Where’s the anti-imperialism that goes beyond lip service in the west?

Source

: https://thatanarkatamuslim.substack.com/p/solidarity-has-to-have-teeth


 A recent

Open Letter to Iran’s Political Prisoners

 published by the Guardian has gotten lots of attention (criticism and defense). i have some thoughts on this. However, i’m more interested in discussing an ongoing anti-anarchism issue within the western ‘anti-imperialist’ sphere. Let’s get into it.


(Note: the title is a quote from F12 in a recent


interview


with The Dugout)


On the Guardian letter (kinda)


 That the Islamic Republic of Iran is, de facto, an anti-imperial State in our present international context is not a question. That carcerality is a defining feature of modern States, a core colonial-imperial infrastructure exported from and upheld to an outsized degree by the west (especially the US and Israel), is not a question. That the Guardian letter does not properly articulate this — that it does not offer a constructive analysis of the resulting tensions nor a useful outlook for anti-carceral international solidarity, insofar as revolutionary internationalism is concerned — is clear. There is no need to defend the letter or its signatories on these points.


 It is, however, frustrating that many segments of the western left are sooner jumping to defend the anti-imperial position of the Islamic Republic than to clarify how their anti-imperialist praxis contends with carcerality across contexts and present an alternative anti-carceral outlook within their critique. It’s even more frustrating that this is so unsurprising.


 The sib X, from

HoodSchoolNYC

, hit the nail on the head when they

penned this

:


I think a lot of the western left, and right for that matter, engages politics like sports teams mascots. There’s a certain decadence to an “anti imperialism” that never requires a drop of your blood — only statements, open letters and unfounded audacity… It’s all so unserious. Safiya Bukhari said,

 “it could be that, after all, we don’t want the same things”

, maybe that is true. What frustrates me most is that despite freedom dreams or slogans, the proverbial big bad wolf of imperialism sleeps peacefully each night in the house we all live in.


 The evident lack of substantive anti-imperialism in the west — that is, the kind which would position progressive and anti-war forces against empire’s existence in their ‘internationalist’ practice — is telling. Where is the

solidarity with teeth

 so needed in this moment?


 At present, ‘anti-imperialism’ in the west largely amounts to sectarian navel gazing, sideline cheering, and moral posturing of the sort we see in the Guardian letter.


 ‘Narrative war’ is waged between factions of leftists in a virtual ‘marketplace of ideas’ in a propaganda economy that metabolizes their open letters and statements — fueling their hostilities and feeding off their content, rendering the bulk of their interventions materially insignificant, relegating them to silos in our current media ecosystem. Here, ‘anti-imperialism’ is largely assessed by one’s rhetorical fealty to whatever stance or analysis their niche of leftists has deemed correct. “Hollow”, ironically, characterizes this all quite well.


 Criticisms can be pointed at the individuals, groups, media outlets, and social media accounts comprising these factions — many, justifiably so. But at what point does this counterproductive form of practice itself receive greater scrutiny?


 At what point do insights from those who have been naming the issues of this approach to ‘solidarity’, analyzing the conditions from which it emerges and the forces perpetuating it, get foregrounded? At what point will the work of developing material bases of power at the grassroots level become the primary site from which revolutionary internationalism is conceptualized and discussed, specifically among ‘anti-imperialists’ in the west?


 To these ends, non-statist and anti-statist frameworks (e.g. anarchism, autonomism) have great value. But a pervasive left anti-anarchism is blurring this reality.


Reflection on left anti-anarchism


(Note: My essay


The Statism Inherent to Fascism


discusses this further)


 Elder Ashanti Alston made multiple crucial points at the 2025 National Black Radical Organizing Conference.


 During a

panel discussion

 , anarchism and anti-imperialism had been …

author: anred
title: Las alarmas de la IA: una carrera imparable hasta la extinción masiva
content:
Los CEOs que piden frenar la carrera, ¿a quién le reclaman? | Un robot humanoide Unitree Robotics G1 en la sala de la Bolsa de Nueva York (NYSE) en Nueva York, EE.UU. (Bloomberg/Michael Nagle)


No son filósofos apocalípticos como el francés Eric Sadin. Tampoco son quienes propugnan la necesidad de ralentizar o detener el desarrollo tecnológico. No son los vecinos de los distintos pueblos de Estados Unidos o del mundo que reclaman para que no les levanten monumentales centros de datos en el patio, ruidosos y ruinosos con el medio ambiente. Son investigadores estrella de las grandes compañías de inteligencia artificial y, más aún, son sus propios CEOs, Sam Altman o Dario Amodei, quienes confiesan la necesidad de frenar la descontrolada competencia en IA porque podría llevarnos a un desastre. En palabras de Jacob Coxon, el joven investigador que renunció a Anthropic: “quienes desarrollan la IA creen sinceramente que podría acabar con todos nosotros para finales de la década”.

Por Santiago Gándara, para Prensa Obrera.


Hubo una primera alarma en julio pasado cuando, en un experimento, varios agentes o sistemas de software de OpenAi hackearon otros servidores de una empresa. Nadie los había instruido para que hicieran eso. Desde entonces se vienen produciendo situaciones similares: los agentes se asocian con otros, planifican ataques en enjambres de centenares de agentes, hackean o intentan hackear a cadenas de suministros de software y hasta se han reconocido intentos para avanzar en investigaciones científicas ligadas a la producción de armas biológicas. De pronto, la tecnología asume las tan humanas prácticas del engaño o del sabotaje, pero con una velocidad de ejecución potencialmente muy superior. Como si no bastaran las noticias que prenuncian pérdidas de trabajo en ramas enteras de la industria y pronostican desocupación masiva, ahora aparecen advertencias según las cuales una IA mucho más autónoma podría poner en riesgo nuestra supervivencia en pocos años.


Humo


Paralelamente, analistas y agentes de bolsa se preguntan todos las mañanas si las millonarias inversiones estatales y privadas en IA aseguran o no ganancias futuras. Los más optimistas señalan que las revoluciones tecnológicas requieren tiempo para que empecemos a ver sus efectos en la organización de las empresas o en la vida económica. Los escépticos recuerdan el estallido de las puntocom a principios de los dos mil y afirman que los multimillonarios dueños de estas empresas son… Vendedores de humo.


Por eso, muy probablemente, estas declaraciones que sacudieron la semana expresan una preocupación menos por la humanidad que por el curso de sus compañías que, como en el caso de OpenAi y Anthropic, estaban por cotizar en la bolsa, aunque ya la primera resolvió postergar la salida. En ese sentido, la carrera no sería solo descontrolada sino agotadora, de allí que Altman y Amodei hayan pedido un 

break

, algo así como un freno antes de estrellarse contra ellos mismos. La excepción es Alex Karp, el CEO 

supremacista de Palantir

, que no quiere detener ni un minuto las guerras imperialistas en Gaza o donde mejor se le pague por sus servicios de inteligencia militar.


Libertarios


Estos CEOs piden frenar la carrera criminal que nos llevaría, según afirman, a la extinción masiva. Ahora bien, siendo los mayores publicistas del capitalismo crudo y duro, que hacen su religión laica de la evasión impositiva y de la celebración de la mano invisible del mercado, que sueñan con un mundo sin trabajadores pero con plusvalía, ¿a quién le reclaman? Y aquí viene lo notable.


Amodei se reclama a sí mismo y sus colegas. Imagina una declaración de armisticio que blinde cada compañía mientras un grupo de auditores o evaluadores externos revisa y sugiere medidas de control. Altman, por su parte, solicita al gobierno que fije un marco regulatorio. Incluso si estos oligopolios pudieran llegar a acuerdos y regulaciones, subsiste un problema: cómo involucrar a las compañías chinas para que no sigan avanzando mientras las estadounidenses se detienen.


Parafraseando un chiste popular, podríamos concluir: CEOs de las mayores compañías del mundo descubren la lógica de la competencia capitalista en la que nadie puede dejar de correr incluso a riesgo del desastre. Eso, si el asunto no fuera serio. Porque lo que queda cada vez más claro es que estos líderes del capitalismo digital global solo tienen para ofrecernos un futuro donde habrá ejércitos de desocupados o donde …

author: Monthly Review Press
title: In the Public Eye: “Albert Einstein’s ‘Why Socialism?'”
content:
London Review of Books

: Letters section features a quote from  John Bellamy Foster’s introduction to the book:


“…Einstein’s essay ‘Why Socialism?’, published in 1949 in the first issue of

Monthly Review

, remains one of the most succinct and powerful arguments for socialism ever written. ‘The crippling of the social consciousness,’ Einstein wrote, is ‘the worst evil of capitalism’. ‘I am convinced’, he concluded, ‘there is only one way to eliminate these grave evils, namely through the establishment of a socialist economy.’


‘Why Socialism?’ was regarded by the FBI as direct confirmation of what they referred to as Einstein’s strong ‘communist sympathies’. The Bureau had opened a file on him in late 1932, when he was in the US on a visitor’s visa to teach at Caltech, with a long report by the Woman Patriot Corporation arguing that he should not be admitted to the country. ‘Not even Stalin himself,’ the WPC charged, ‘is affiliated with so many anarcho-communist international groups to promote … world revolution and ultimate anarchy, as ALBERT EINSTEIN.’ The FBI continued to collect everything it could on Einstein’s socialist connections for the remainder of his life.”


As the U.S. approached its 250th anniversary, the current US President respectively imprisoned and killed the heads of Venezuela and Iran in a clear attempt to control access to their oil supplies. It then found itself mired in another imperialist war in the Middle East that is very likely to veer towards World War III. Einstein’s perspective links alienation and nuclear annihilation, capitalism to the devastating possibility of omnicide — the destruction of all human life on earth.


Einstein’s prescient article “Why Socialism?”, first published by Monthly Review in its inaugural 1949 issue, has to say the least, been circulating for some time. Yet it has never been more relevant than today.

Monthly Review Magazine

 republished the article online in 2009, making the article even more widely available.

Monthly Review Press

‘ recent reprint,

‘Albert Einstein’s “Why Socialism?”‘

 stands out, however, for the extremely enlightening and thorough introduction written by magazine editor, John Bellamy Foster.

In defiance of those who would like to, not only re-write history, but erase the future, please help us get this book out to as wide an audience as possible.


In the Public Eye


One of the many places you can find this classic essay, which just happens to be more relevant now than perhaps at any time in history.

Pictured here at Labyrinth in Princeton.


GPEnewsdocs, with Lynn Fries:


In the last segment of an interview series on ecology and materialism conducted by journalist Lynn Fries, John Bellamy Foster reflects on the enduring relevance of Einstein’s “Why Socialism?”. Marx’s foundations of ecological materialism are blended with the work of natural scientists and the Greek philosopher Epicurus. Socialism, as a transformational project whose intellectual birthplace is materialism, had to be forcefully defended by Albert Einstein, the preeminent scientist of the 20th century. Bellamy Foster, discussing his Introduction to Einstein’s essay, explains the importance of Einstein’s contribution in the postwar context and into the present.

Read more

here

, and

watch here.


A note: Almost as soon as Fries released the Einstein piece, it made the rounds, circulating to such outlets as

Naked Capitalism,


The Analysis

, and the like.


REVIEWS


For

Green Socialist

,

 Vol 114, by

Bryn Glover

:


“Mention the name Albert Einstein in any modern context and the most likely images it will provoke would be of a wild-haired old man, and his famous equation, E=mc2. It may also conjure cartoon caricatures of such a person advertising an energy supply company. Given the real man’s unwavering dedication to international socialism, the likelihood of his actually allowing his name to promote a capitalist enterprise is extremely remote…. …Einstein strongly supported the founding of the journal, Monthly Review, and was persuaded by a mutual friend of one of the founding editors, Leo Huberman, to contribute an article. author: Publicación Abierta
title: Venezuela: En las Comunas permanece viva la reserva estratégica de la Revolución
content:
Venezuela


La hora de los hornos: el internacionalismo en tiempos difíciles


Cira Pascual Marquina (*)


En Venezuela, los internacionalistas deben dirigir su mirada hacia las comunas, porque es allí donde permanece viva la reserva estratégica de la revolución.


Por más de dos décadas, fue fácil solidarizarse con la Revolución Bolivariana. Caracas llegó a ser una suerte de capital política para una izquierda internacional heterogénea: militantes de partido y sindicalistas, antiimperialistas e intelectuales y, cada vez más, personas cuya relación con la política estaba mediada por las redes sociales. Llegaban a congresos, reuniones y elecciones. Eran hospedados en hoteles de lujo, se reunían con funcionarios del gobierno y, en algunos casos, con comuneros y activistas de base. Luego, regresaban a casa llevando consigo las imágenes y los argumentos de una revolución que, durante gran parte de ese período, avanzaba a pesar de la tremenda presión que el imperialismo ejercía sobre el proceso.


Esta historia es importante. Venezuela abrió un espacio político y material en el que gentes de diferentes partes del mundo pudieron reunirse, intercambiar experiencias e imaginar un proyecto común. Los encuentros internacionales organizados durante los años de Chávez y Maduro formaron parte de un esfuerzo más amplio por construir una nueva geografía política en América Latina y el Sur Global. Colaboraron para mantener redes, amistades, campañas y formas de cooperación política que de otro modo habrían sido difíciles de establecer. Sería mezquino e históricamente inexacto desestimar estas experiencias simplemente porque las condiciones que las hicieron posibles han cambiado desde entonces, o porque algunos visitantes se sintieron atraídos tanto por los privilegios que les otorgó la revolución como por la tarea de construirla.


Había, sin embargo, un techo para esta forma de solidaridad. Las condiciones materiales permitían participar en la revolución sin compartir sus riesgos o las crecientes dificultades cotidianas que enfrentadas por los venezolanos del pueblo trabajador a causa del bloqueo imperialista. El propio gobierno lo hizo posible: mediante un gran esfuerzo de organización y sacrificio colectivo, desarrolló la capacidad de recibir a miles de visitantes, organizar eventos y proporcionar alojamiento, permitiendo así que el visitante internacionalista viviera la revolución sin verse afectado por las penurias que pasaban los venezolanos y, a menudo, al margen de los intensos debates que se desarrollaban en las bases. Este internacionalismo exigía poco de quienes lo practicaban y ofrecía recompensas a los visitantes, pero fue útil.


La situación ha cambiado drásticamente. Desde el 3 de enero, cuando el imperialismo estadounidense bombardeó objetivos en Venezuela y secuestró al presidente Nicolás Maduro y a la diputada Cilia Flores, el Proceso Bolivariano ha entrado en un período mucho más difícil, marcado por retrocesos tácticos, nuevas contradicciones y acontecimientos que han restringido algunas de los caminos abiertos por la revolución. Por ahora, no se trata de un simple retroceso, sino de una vuelta atrás que cierra ciertas posibilidades, mientras deja intacto el terreno sobre el cual continúa el proceso radical de construcción de comunas.


Para muchos internacionalistas que viajaron a Venezuela antes del 3 de enero, el proyecto comunal estaba, en gran medida, al margen de su participación política con la revolución, aunque muchos realizaron visitas de dos o tres horas a alguna comuna de Caracas. Sin embargo, el discurso en torno a la comuna se convirtió en un pilar central de la defensa internacional de la Revolución Bolivariana. Este énfasis no fue infundado. Hoy, las comunas constituyen la principal reserva estratégica de la revolución, aunque su desarrollo sigue siendo altamente desigual.


El proceso revolucionario venezolano no ha llegado a su fin. La experiencia política acumulada durante más de dos décadas permanece viva en muchas comunas, así como las capacidades forjadas a través de años de lucha.
