title: Indien: Helfen Sie Elefant Madhuri zurück in die Auffangstation
content:
Videoinhalt: © PETA India


Elefantendame

 Madhuri verbrachte jahrzehntelang angekettet und isoliert in einem Kloster (Matha) in Indien. Nach Bemühungen von PETA Indien wurde sie im Juli 2025 auf Anordnung eines Sonderausschusses des Obersten Gerichtshofs von Indien (High-Powered Committee, HPC) und des Obersten Gerichtshofs von Bombay aus ihrer tierquälerischen Haltung in das Elefanten-Rehabilitationszentrum Vantara gebracht. Dort erhielt sie tiermedizinische Versorgung, konnte erstmals Kontakt zu anderen Elefantinnen aufnehmen und begann, sich körperlich und psychisch zu erholen.  


Am 9. September 2026 ordnete das HPC jedoch an, dass die Elefantendame in dasselbe Kloster zurückkehren muss, in dem sie über Jahrzehnte unter den belastenden Haltungsbedingungen litt. 


Warum wurde Madhuri in die schlechte Haltung zurückgebracht? 

 


Dem Beschluss vom 9. September ging eine Kehrtwende Vantaras voraus. Die Organisation erklärte, Madhuris weiterer Aufenthalt in der Einrichtung liege nicht länger „im Interesse von Madhuri oder des Klosters“. Diese Kursänderung folgte einer Kampagne, die die Rückführung von Madhuri forderte und zum Boykott von Produkten aufrief, die mit dem Unternehmen hinter Vantara verbunden sind.  


Drei Monate vor der Entscheidung berichtete Vantaras Veterinärteam selbst, dass Madhuri mit schweren chronischen Erkrankungen angekommen sei. Die Folgen schlechter Haltung seien deutlich sichtbar gewesen, weshalb sie fortlaufend spezialisierte Behandlungen und regelmäßige Kontrollen benötige. 


Rückführung ins Kloster bedeutet enorme Risiken für Elefantendame Madhuri 

 


Während der jahrzehntelangen Haltung im Kloster war Madhuri gezwungen, fast regungslos auf Betonboden im Tempel zu leben. Dadurch hat sie irreversible gesundheitliche Schäden erlitten, darunter eine chronische Fußerkrankung und Arthritis. Die Rückführung birgt deshalb erhebliche Risiken für die Elefantendame. Sie benötigt weiterhin spezialisierte tiermedizinische Versorgung, die sie im Kloster nicht bekommen kann. Zudem hat sie nach 33 Jahren Isolation erstmals enge soziale Bindungen zu anderen Elefantinnen aufbauen können, die durch die Rückführung erneut zerstört wurden.  


Erst wenige Wochen zuvor hatten vom Sonderausschuss HPC eingesetzte Inspektoren das Kloster besucht. Ihr Fazit: Die Anlage sei für eine langfristige Haltung ungeeignet. Dennoch wurde Madhuri Mitte September 2026, nach nur 13 Monaten im Rehabilitationszentrum Vantara, wieder in den Tempel in Kolhapur überführt. 


PETA Indien setzt sich weiterhin dafür ein, dass Madhuri zurück in die Rehabilitationseinrichtung von Vantara gebracht wird.  


Fordern Sie jetzt Madhuris Rückkehr in die Auffangstation 

 


Elefantendame Madhuri musste zurück in eine Umgebung, die ihren Bedürfnissen als Wildtier niemals gerecht wird. Sie braucht dringend medizinische Versorgung, den Kontakt zu Artgenossen und die Möglichkeit, in einer geeigneten Umgebung zu leben. Unterstützen Sie deshalb PETA Indiens Petition und fordern Sie die Verantwortlichen auf, Madhuri dauerhaft in der Rehabilitationseinrichtung von Vantara unterzubringen. 


Jetzt Madhuri helfen (Weiterleitung auf PETA India)


The post

Indien: Helfen Sie Elefant Madhuri zurück in die Auffangstation 

 appeared first on

PETA Deutschland e.V.

.

author: webadmin
title: Quantock Hunt Members Charged
content:
At long last, charges have been issued against members of a stag hunt. 


Huntsman Martin Watts. Image Credit Mendip Hunt Sabs


Avon and Somerset Police have charged Quantock Staghounds hunt master Chris Gibbons and huntsman Martin Watts with illegally hunting a wild mammal with dogs in relation to an incident on March 16, 2026.


Watts faces a further charge relating to a separate incident on April 23, 2026.


Both men are to appear in Taunton Magistrates’ Court on October 22, 2026 to answer the charges.


Hunt master Chris Gibbons. Image credit North Dorset Hunt Saboteurs


The charges follow what was, for a stag hunt, an ordinary day in March, when hunt saboteurs from Mendip Hunts Sabs and North Dorset Hunt Sabs were in attendance and recorded events as they unfolded.


The stag was first seen by sabs at around noon

. It would be almost six o’clock before the day was over and the stag was dead.


For more than five hours sabs documented the pursuit as the animal repeatedly fled. Quads, hunters on horseback, hounds and even motorbikes were involved as the stag attempted to escape.


It is difficult to comprehend what five hours of pursuit actually means for the animal. Deer are not endurance runners, prolonged exertion can cause severe physiological stress and overheating, and exhausted deer often enter rivers or streams during or following a pursuit.


The stag was pursued for over five-hours


Spring stag hunting takes place from early March until late April. Younger stags without the heavy antlers and greater body mass they develop later in the year, have historically been prized by stag hunters for the speed of the chase.


It is the pursuit itself, the flight of the wild animal turned into entertainment for bloodthirsty baying hunters.


Eventually after a gruelling five-hour pursuit the exhausted stag was trapped against a fence line with a sab on the other side.


The image of the stag was haunting. His jaw was bloodied and visibly deformed, his eyes bulging and blood pouring from his nose. His body was cut and gashed after hours of desperate flight across the landscape.


The haunting image of the stag moments before death, as a Mendip Hunt Sab begged for the animal to be left alone


What the sabs witnessed that day has left a mental scar, while the haunting video they managed to record has also stayed with many who have watched it.


As one sab desperately begged for the exhausted and injured stag to be left alone, hunters laughed as they raced past with the gun, demonstrating the stark contrast between the compassion of the sab pleading for mercy, and the barbarity of the hunters frothing and chewing at the bit to get their kill.


Soon after, the stag was dead.


Huntsman Martin Watts at the Quantock Staghounds’ closing meet 2026. Image Credit North Dorset Hunt Saboteurs


Watts’ second charge relates to an incident on April 23, 2026 during the Quantock Staghounds’ closing meet at Bagborough.


Hunting Act exemptions are subject to specific conditions, such as having permission to be on the land they are on.


The hunt was filmed by monitors from Wildlife Guardian hunting a young stag through Triscombe Quarry, a dangerous working quarry, which sabs say they had no permission to enter.


This time, unlike the stag pursued on March 16, he escaped alive. Eventually making his way into New Ground, a League Against Cruel Sport sanctuary.


The Quantock Staghounds are no strangers to seeing one of their huntsmen before the courts. Former QSH huntsman, Richard Down, was convicted in 2007 after

hunting a deer for more than an hour

. He was convicted again in 2010 for hunting a wild mammal with more than two dogs.


Down, who was still huntsman of the Quantock Staghounds at the time, became the first

huntsman to be convicted twice

 under the Hunting Act.


An HSA spokesperson said:


“These charges are a testament to the extraordinary dedication of the hunt saboteurs and monitors who spend countless hours in the field documenting what happens at stag hunts.


The Hunting Act must be strengthened to remove the exemptions, loopholes and excuses that hunts rely on to get away with the traditional hunting of wildlife with dogs.


This stag was chased for more than five-hours. We have been waiting 22 years for the law to catch up”.


You can support Mendip Hunt Sabs

here

 and North Dorset Hunt Sabs

here

.

Quantock Hunt Members Charged

 appeared first on

Hunt Saboteurs Association

.

Packham stepped down as president of the RSPCA in December 2024 following Animal Rising investigations into RSPCA Assured farms and slaughterhouses, saying he had seen “no meaningful change” in response to the findings. [5] [6]

Michelle Farnham has spent years examining conditions inside British animal farms. She studied Animal Management for two years and has since reviewed hundreds of hours of undercover footage recorded inside UK pig farms, working alongside veterinary and animal welfare law experts to assess conditions, including during Animal Rising’s investigations into RSPCA Assured farms and slaughterhouses.

Farrowing crates can confine mother pigs for four to five weeks at a time around giving birth and nursing their piglets, leaving them unable to turn around or take more than a step forward or back. Sows are put through this cycle repeatedly, returning to the crates with successive litters until they are eventually culled.

Animal Rising released its investigation into Luna’s life last week, after documenting her for a month on a factory farm in Suffolk. Hidden-camera footage narrated by Michelle shows Luna giving birth and nursing her piglets while confined inside a farrowing crate, unable to turn around or freely interact with her piglets. Animal Rising is calling for Luna to be released to a sanctuary home that has been offered to her, alongside its wider call for the Government to commit to ending factory farming by 2040.

Onze mille cinq cents oiseaux aquatiques y sont enfermés sur un caillebotis de plastique, sans litière, sans aucun dispositif leur permettant de plonger la tête dans l'eau. On les mutile pour qu'ils arrivent à survivre assez longtemps dans ces conditions ; Ils arrivent dans l'élevage le bec épointé. Leurs griffes sont coupées. Au ramassage, ils sont empoignés brutalement par le cou et balancés dans les caisses de transport.

Votre charte éthique fournisseurs engage pourtant chacun de vos fournisseurs à respecter les réglementations en matière de bien-être animal et à bannir les actes de cruauté envers les animaux.

Ces images ont été filmées en juillet et en août 2026 dans un élevage de canards de Barbarie de Sèvremoine, dans le Maine-et-Loire. 11 500 oiseaux y sont enfermés dans un seul bâtiment fermé.

author: webdev@democracynow.org (Democracy Now!)
title: Nepali Activist at U.N. Rally Calls for Climate Justice After Deadly Glacier Floods Kill Thousands
content:
In the wake of devastating flash floods triggered by glacial collapse in the Himalayas, Nepal is demanding climate reparations from polluter countries as it embarks upon the grueling process of rebuilding. Over 1,400 bodies have been recovered from the disaster, with around 6,000 others still missing. Nepal’s government estimates that the cost of infrastructure reconstruction is likely to exceed $4 billion. Nepal contributes less than 0.1% of global carbon emissions, yet as a mountainous country surrounded by glaciers, continues to be vulnerable to the effects of climate change. Recent studies estimate that global surface temperatures will likely exceed 1.5°C above preindustrial levels by the end of the decade.


We go to a rally outside of United Nations headquarters, where Nepali activists, including our guest Anisha Buda, are demanding climate justice, reparations and a just transition out of fossil fuels. Buda, a member of the region’s ethnic minority Kaike-speaking Magar community, says that almost 90% of the victims impacted by August’s flash flooding were part of Nepal’s Indigenous communities. “It is not just the lives of the people lost. It’s not just the houses swept, but it’s their culture, tradition and their very identity that is being lost by the floods, by the climate-induced disasters.”

author: Unknown
title: Pasture bans: Rural decline and a new wave of forced migration
content:
Security-driven policies pursued for decades in Northern Kurdistan (Bakur) are gradually dismantling livestock farming, the main source of livelihood for the rural population. Restrictions on access to pastures on military grounds, the designation of grazing areas as “special security zones” and measures preventing villagers from taking their animals into the mountains and highland pastures are effectively bringing an end to a way of life that has sustained the people of Kurdistan for thousands of years. This is not accidental, but the result of a deliberate, systematic and political choice.


Small and large livestock farming, the backbone of the rural economy in Kurdistan, has come under an increasingly restrictive regime in recent years. Villagers can no longer freely take their animals to highland pastures. Even where access is permitted, they face narrow corridors imposed on security grounds, constant identity checks and arbitrary entry bans. These restrictions have gone far beyond a question of access. They amount to a deliberate severing of the ties between local people, their land and their economic autonomy.


Highland pasture bans are often imposed without any specific justification, in the middle of the grazing season and without prior notice. For a farmer, even a few weeks without access to pasture can mean losing an entire year’s livestock. Villagers are therefore forced either to sell their animals early at a loss or to abandon livestock farming altogether.


Highland pastures closed on ‘security’ grounds


The roots of today’s pasture and highland bans can be traced back to the village evacuations and state of emergency measures of the 1990s. Thousands of villages and hamlets were evacuated by state forces during that period, uprooting people from their land. The same logic now continues in a more “civilian” form. Villages are no longer being evacuated, but the pastures on which villagers depend for their livelihoods are effectively being made inaccessible. The outcome is the same: people are separated from their land and grazing grounds, reshaping the region’s demographic and economic structure.


Preferential access to some pastures for village guards, while villagers without ties to the state are excluded, further deepens inequality in the region. Pastureland thus ceases to function as a shared natural resource and becomes a privilege distributed on the basis of loyalty and obedience.


Signs of a collapsing economy


Regional chambers of agriculture and professional organisations have repeatedly said in statements to the press that livestock numbers have fallen sharply across the region over the past two decades, with livestock farming almost disappearing in many villages. Villages once known for their herds have become settlements where only an ageing population remains and agricultural production has largely ceased. Younger generations no longer see staying in their villages as a viable option because they have little opportunity to continue their families’ livelihoods.


The collapse of livestock farming means more than a loss of income. It also threatens the disappearance of centuries of knowledge and a deeply rooted way of life. Seasonal migration to highland pastures, herd management and traditions of communal use formed a system of social organisation passed down from one generation to the next. This way of life has rapidly eroded as access to pastures has effectively been eliminated.


A new route of migration from the highlands to the cities


Migration is becoming the only option for rural families who have lost their livelihoods. Unlike the forced mass evacuations of the 1990s, this process may appear more “voluntary”, but it is no less imposed by circumstances. Families are moving to the outskirts of cities such as Diyarbakır (Amed), Van (Wan), Urfa (Riha) and Mardin (Mêrdîn), or to major cities outside Northern Kurdistan, where they often struggle to survive through insecure, low-paid and seasonal work.


This wave of migration is creating new pockets of poverty and marginalisation in urban centres. Families who were producers in the countryside become a source of cheap labour in the cities, while the autonomous relationship they once had with their land, livestock and natural environment is replaced by a precarious struggle for survival in impoverished urban neighbourhoods. The process goes beyond individual impoverishment and amounts to a broader social uprooting.

author: Keelan Jacobs
title: AFN National Chief warns Ottawa not to rush Bill C-39 or West Coast pipeline
content:
National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak says the federal government should not designate a proposed West Coast oil pipeline a project of national interest until First Nations in its path can decide for themselves, or use its majority in the House of Commons to cut off debate on the new major-projects bill tabled the night before. 


Woodhouse Nepinak said the Assembly of First Nations (AFN) received the Building Canada Strong Act (Bill C-39) only last night and that her lawyers are still reviewing it. Regional chiefs meet this week, and AFN will release a full assessment after that.


Ottawa has called C-39, an omnibus bill with several sections, affecting different topics, among the most consequential bills in decades, she said. 


“We warn the government against abusing its majority status and dishonoring the Crown through procedural tools, time allocation or closure to frustrate Parliament’s ability to hear from rights holders and consider amendments,” she said. 


She linked the bill to a proposal to designate Alberta’s West Coast oil pipeline a project of national interest. That project, she said, has the potential to impact more than 100 First Nation communities.

 


“The Assembly of First Nations is requesting that no national interest designation be given to this project until meaningful engagement and decision-making protocols have been fully considered with affected First Nations.” 


Once a project is designated, she said, environmental assessments that create room for dialogue can be bypassed. 


A

Canada-Alberta implementation agreement

 already points to a national-interest designation by Oct. 1 and conditions by Sept. 1, 2027 — a timeline set before consultation is done. A timeline set before consultations with affected First Nations is complete, she said. 


“Any predetermined timeline principally designed to attract investment subordinates the honor of the Crown to commercial imperatives.” 


Asked if one year is enough to consult, she said Nations need as much time as they need. “One year’s tight.”


She compared the pace to last year’s C-5 process, which she said moved in about 20 days while chiefs who wanted to testify stood outside Parliament Hill. 


Woodhouse was critical of the Major Projects Office, a group assembled by Prime Minister Mark Carney to fast track “projects of national interest.” The office is based in Calgary. 


Woodhouse said the AFN invited

Major Projects Office CEO Dawn Farrell

 to address chiefs in assembly – but she didn’t show up. The national chief said “junior staff” were sent instead. 


“If you’re too good to come and talk to our chiefs, stay home then,” she said. “Stay in Calgary.”

 


Read More:


Legislation that gives feds sweeping power over national projects passes in House of Commons 


When asked if she’d support the pipeline being designated as being in the public interest, Woodhouse Nepinak said it’s not for her to decide.


“That’s up to the chiefs in assembly. If they give us that mandate, we will. And if they don’t, we’ll stand with them as well,” she said.


Woodhouse said AFN expects to get a briefing on the bill at 11am Tuesday. A written breakdown for First Nations, she said, will follow in the coming days. 


Woodhouse said the fall sitting must also end the Indian Act’s second-generation cut-off. Bill S-2 does just that.


Imagine being told you are First Nations, she said, and then being told your child is not. 


“Nobody else in the country would have to deal with that. No other group of people except First Nations people, and we have to get this right once and for all together.”


Bill S-2

 is one of many important issues on the radar of AFN’s National Chief that affect First Nations people across Canada.

author: Sophia Sheera
title: Greta Thunberg Is Taking Sweden to Court Over Climate Crisis Again
content:
Greta Thunberg and Swedish youth climate organisation Aurora are suing the Swedish government over its failures to tackle the climate crisis.


While Sweden has reduced its greenhouse gas emissions at a rate faster than the EU average, the country is

not on track

 to meet its own target of net zero by 2045.  


Thunberg said on Monday that Aurora has filed a second

 lawsuit

, arguing that Sweden is failing in its legal duty to protect its citizens – especially children and the young – from the effects of climate change.


The group is demanding that Sweden take action to limit global warming to 1.5C by cutting emissions and protecting ecosystems like forests. A third demand involves accounting for emissions that it says are currently excluded from government calculations such as burning imported biomass.


“Sweden, as a rich country with high historical and current emissions, has a legal duty to lead the climate transition,”

the group wrote in its fundraiser

. “A safe and just world is still possible, but only if rich, high-emitting states like Sweden stop violating their duty to protect people from the devastation of the climate crisis, and start transforming their societies before 2030.” 


Thunberg and Aurora’s first attempt to sue Sweden into taking stronger action against climate change was

quashed in February

, when the country’s supreme court decreed it could not force the government to take action. 


However, the Swedish court did not rule out that a differently formulated claim might have better success. In 2024, the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR)

said

 that citizens can sue governments that fail to tackle climate change, on the grounds that their right to a private and family life could be violated by climate breakdown. 


Civil groups have successfully sued their governments in the

Netherlands

,

Belgium

,

Germany

 and

Switzerland

, forcing them to take more drastic measures to protect the environment. 


Thunberg and campaigners at Aurora have so far

raised more than £180k

 to fund their forthcoming lawsuit.

author: James McVicar
title: Why do the Greens always chicken out?
content:
When Larissa Waters was elected leader of the Australian Greens, she said she was there to “

get shit done

”.

True to her word, Waters did something last week—and it was, indeed, shit. Greens MPs gave

crucial support

 in the Senate to the roll-out of a carbon emissions offset scheme so bad that the term “greenwashing” seems generous.

Under the scheme, state governments will now be able to take publicly owned forest, promise not to deforest it, and then convert that promise into “carbon credits”. These credits can then be sold to greenhouse gas emitters to subtract from their overall carbon emissions count.

In NSW, the scheme is being tied to the establishment of a 476,000-hectare koala reserve the state government had already promised back in 2015. This move, according to Larissa Waters, put the Greens in an “

impossible position

” and forced them to support Labor’s carbon credit scam.

So now, in exchange for doing something it had already said it would do, the NSW Labor government can continue to do

nothing

 to trees that were

already there

 and, in turn, magically generate permits for carbon emitters to carry on emitting carbon.

The Greens are now trying to sell this as a step forward for the planet, Waters describing it as the “first chink in the armour of coal and gas”.

Cartoonist First Dog on the Moon found a

visual metaphor

 much nearer the mark, depicting a Labor MP holding a cuddly koala at gunpoint and threatening the Greens leader: “vote for climate change or the koala gets it”.

Richard Denniss of the Australia Institute—hardly a radical left outfit—likened the Greens decision to “

fiddling while the forest burns

”. He went on: “In voting with Labor, the Greens ... have tied the protection of trees and koalas to the expansion of gas and coal”.

Labor’s actions come as no surprise, given the party’s longstanding support for Australia’s fossil fuel industry. But why the hell have the Greens gone along with it?

Prominent left-wing Greens figure Jonathan Sriranganathan criticised his party but suggested it was simply a problem of accountability. In a recent

Facebook post

 about the carbon credit vote, he wrote:

“Despite having plenty of time and capacity to do so, the three federal Greens politicians in Queensland didn’t bother seeking out the views of all the people who helped get them elected.”

To be sure, in a party whose sole purpose is to accrue seats in parliament, MPs usually dominate decision-making with little rank-and-file oversight. But internal democracy within the Australian Greens, however scant it may be, is not the real problem.

For one thing, there’s no evidence that Greens members overwhelmingly oppose the way their MPs voted in the Senate, though undoubtedly many do. Even Sriranganathan didn’t venture to say in his post that the Greens MPs who did so were wrong to support the bill.

What it comes down to is politics.

The Greens are a pro-capitalist party. They may not like some of its worst aspects, but the party has never been for overturning the system. They are committed to working within it.

The contradictions of such a project are perhaps most obvious on the question that is so core to the party’s political identity: climate change.

The Greens insist the climate crisis can be tackled without any radical change to the way our society operates. Rejecting any fundamental alternative to the profit-driven logic of capitalism, they instead throw their support behind farcical “market solutions” that shield the fossil fuel industry from real action.

And even when the Greens are critical of greenwashing scams, they aren’t willing to put up a fight lest they be accused of obstructing or “letting the perfect be the enemy of the good”. This isn’t just poor strategy; it stems from wanting to be seen as responsible partners in government.

These endless acrobatics of compromise also send the wrong message to Greens supporters and left-wing people more broadly. Party leaders have to run PR for every shoddy deal they stitch up with Labor, no matter how bad, and sell it as progress. Anyone who disagrees is a helpless idealist, a useful idiot for the side of “perfect” against the side of “good”.

Socialist politics offers an alternative. Socialists never limit our demands to what is palatable to the rich parasites who run this country and their defenders in parliament.

We know that radical social change is possible and that it doesn’t come from parliamentary manoeuvring …

author: Dominic Gutoman
title: ‘Human rights reparation starts with justice’
content:
Portraits of enforced disappearance victims. Photo by Dominic Gutoman/Bulatlat.

MANILA – All human rights violation victims should receive reparation consistent with domestic laws and international obligations.

“From a victim-oriented perspective, the State must recognize that different human rights violations may require various kinds of reparations based on the demands of the victims, their families, and communities which they belong to, to correct the wrongs and achieve healing,” the 2026 Commission on Human Rights (CHR) position paper stated. “Essentially, reparation should be proportional to the gravity of the violations committed and the extent of harm suffered.”

“When my daughter was killed, we received no single assistance nor investigation from the authorities. Not the barangay, not the police. Not one from the government offered help,” Sally Ramos told Bulatlat. Her daughter was killed in 2017 by four unidentified men at the height of the anti-drug campaign.

She said, “We are poor, I do not have a job. My daughter who was killed had a job before she was killed. She supported us for our daily needs and in taking care of my two grandchildren. That is why it was hard for me to accept her passing.”

Read: Ten years on, Duterte’s kill order strikes deep

While it supports the passage of Human Rights Violations Victims Compensations Act (House Bill No. 580), CHR recommends a harmonized definition of victims of human rights violations as persons whose human rights were violated by persons acting in an official capacity and by agents of the State, as well as due to the State’s failure to perform its obligations to prevent, investigate, punish, and redress the private actors’ abuse.

However, human rights group Karapatan disagreed with the bill’s definition that human rights violations are committed by “State or Non-State actors.”

“States are duty-bearers of rights and as such have obligations under international human rights law far greater than non-State actors, and thus the term ‘human rights violations’ should pertain to those committed by State actors. Meanwhile, those allegedly committed by Non-State actors are considered offenses against persons and as such are covered by provisions under criminal and civil laws,” Karapatan Secretary-General Cristina Palabay said.

The existing Victims Compensation Program under Republic Act 7309 provides reparation for martial law victims-survivors. The proposed bill complements this, covering cases and victims that fall outside the scope of RA 7309, particularly those involving indirect State responsibility, non-state actors, or failures of State protection.

“Acknowledging the HRVs committed against the victims is an essential step toward healing, community reconciliation, and justice. This measure will not only affirm the rights of the victims, but will also ensure that acts of grave injustice and abuse will be legally penalized and no victims, regardless of the nature of the violation, will be left disregarded,” the CHR said.

“Compensation could be a big help for the victims’ families, especially if those killed or disappeared were the breadwinners of their families” Cora Jazmines said. Her husband James, a labor rights defender, was forcibly disappeared on August 23, 2024 around 10 p.m., after celebrating the birthday of his friend, Felix Salaveria, Jr. It was Salaveria who reported James’ disappearance. Five days later, Salaveria was also abducted. Both of them remain missing.

Jazmines was among the signatories of a letter to the Supreme Court, urging them to review the writs of amparo and habeas data this August 2026. The court granted the petition for writ of amparo but it has not yielded positive results for their search.

Read: Not one surfaced despite court orders, families demand review of legal remedies

“The majority of Filipino families struggle to make ends meet. As a result, many of the issues raised by HRV victims center on advancing and protecting the basic rights of citizens, including access to adequate food, decent wages and livelihoods, quality education, housing, and healthcare services,” Jazmines said, stressing that if the primary breadwinner of the family was subjected to state violence, the family left behind can be pushed even deeper into poverty.

The bill has been pending with the House Committee on Human Rights since July 29, 2025. The State’s duty to provide reparation is also stated in the International Covenant on Civil and …

author: Kay Pacha / Equipo Pueblos Originarios del SERPAJ
title: La bronca de los Pueblos Originarios
content:
El sábado pasado, 19 de septiembre, se llevó a cabo en una gran cantidad de ciudades del país, la denominada “Marcha de la bronca”, organizada principalmente por sectores de izquierda, pero cuyos objetivos fueron asumidos por una gran parte de la población.


https://argentina.indymedia.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Marcha-de-la-Bronca-termindo.mp3


https://argentina.indymedia.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Marcha-de-la-Bronca-termindo.mp3


Descargar audio


Porque es eso, una gran parte de la población del país está enojada, molesta, decepcionada y fundamentalmente desesperanzada, por la situación económica, social y política que está atravesando el país.


Y por supuesto, dentro de esa gran parte, se encuentran los pueblos originarios. Porque si bien vienen soportando injusticias desde hace tiempo, es ahora donde la situación ya llegó a su punto máximo.


Donde ya no se encuentra ningún atisbo de justicia y de recurso adónde hacer valer sus derechos. Fundamentalmente el derecho a su territorio y a sus bienes naturales, en y con los que han vivido desde hace muchos años, ancestralmente diríamos.


Sus territorios, tan respetados y cuidados, ahora son objeto de la avaricia de terratenientes y empresas extractivas, a los que sólo les importa correrlos de esos lugares tan codiciados. En esos lugares donde el agua es un recurso y un bien muy preciado, y que en muchos lugares escasea por eso se lo cuida tanto.  Las inmobiliarias, las mineras, las empresas madereras, todas ellas, sólo quieren correr a las comunidades de sus lugares para poder instalarse y hacer sus negocios cómodamente.


No les importa el derecho ancestral, no les importa el derecho de la Madre Tierra y mucho menos los derechos de los humanos. Por todas estas situaciones, es que muchos hermanos y hermanas apoyaron, invitaron y participaron de esta marcha de la bronca, porque ellos también tienen que expresarse y tienen que denunciar las situaciones de injusticia que vienen soportando.


Si bien han participado en muchos espacios, aquí vamos a escuchar a algunos hermanos y hermanas que estuvieron en Ciudad de Buenos Aires, Jujuy, Río Negro y Neuquén. Agradecemos a las hermanas de Telesisa y a FARCO, por los materiales que pudimos utilizar. Pedimos disculpas a nuestros oyentes si algunos audios no se escuchan tan bien, porque se grabaron al aire libre y en medio de una multitud.


El Micro Kay Pacha se realiza con el apoyo de la organización Otto per Mille-Chiessa Valdense.

author: M.P
title: Temuco: Filmoteca Ufro presentará su libro “Memorias en movimiento”
content:
Dos años en el desafío de mediar, catalogar, digitalizar y difundir más de 3 mil rollos cinematográficos, tras la adjudicación del fondo de Salvaguardia del Patrimonio Audiovisual del Ministerio de las Culturas, las Artes y el Patrimonio, es lo que compiló Filmoteca Ufro en su libro “Memorias en movimiento”. La presentación será este miércoles 23 de septiembre a las 17:00 horas, en el Auditorio Selva Saavedra de la Universidad de La Frontera.

En el segundo piso de la Biblioteca Central de la Universidad de la Frontera, frente a la escalera, se encuentra la Filmoteca Ufro. Una sala pequeña donde habitan cámaras filmadoras y cintas de diversos formatos, que “posibilitaron la captura de la memoria”, como le gusta decir a Diego Olivares, periodista, tipógrafo, realizador y archivista audiovisual que coordina este proyecto.

El origen de este archivo fílmico se sitúa en el 2008, cuando Diego se encontraba realizando un documental cuyo protagonista no tenía imágenes de su infancia, por lo que juntaron cerca de cien latas de películas. ”El acuerdo era construir su historia con imágenes de otros niños, con imágenes encontradas que servirían para retratar otra época: las calles, los autos, la moda, los roles de género”, relata.

De cientos de rollos pasaron a miles, lo que comenzó a ser un problema para un coleccionista por la falta de un lugar adecuado para resguardarlos. Años después, Diego Olivares logró hacer un vínculo con la Universidad de la Frontera -donde es docente- para almacenarlos.

Uno de los principales hallazgos en este crecimiento, tiene lugar en el Persa Bío Bío de Santiago, donde Diego se encontraba vitrineando cuando llamaron su atención unas latas escasamente rotuladas en las que podía leer “Budi, Puerto Saavedra”. Volvió a Temuco con 26 latas de cine en 16 mm. filmadas entre 1926 y 1936, lo que resultó ser una sorpresa, porque el modelo de cámaras usadas para su filmación comenzó a ser vendido en el mundo tan solo tres años antes de hechos estos registros en la costa de la Araucanía, por parte de la familia ganadera Duhalde, de origen Vasco Francés. Dato de origen al que llegaron gracias a la observación del profesor Jaime Flores de la Ufro, quien identificó un tipo de ganado particular que se aprecia en algunas de estas cintas.

El 2024 Filmoteca Ufro fue el único proyecto no metropolitano en adjudicarse este fondo para la Salvaguardia del Patrimonio Audiovisual, sin embargo, Diego Olivares destaca la importancia nacional de este trabajo, ya que las imágenes que conservan son desde el norte hasta el sur más extremo de Chile: “Creemos que es un gran aporte a nivel nacional, porque hay muchos lugares que solo están filmados en estos pequeños formatos. Muchas veces el Estado, el cine nacional, propagandístico, político, el cine más comercial no llegó a todos los lugares, porque nuestro cine ha estado súper inconcluso”.

Uno de los pilares de la instalación de Filmoteca Ufro es el programa de mediación que ha relacionado a las comunidades interesadas con el acervo y la labor de este archivo. El artista y realizador audiovisual Ange Cayuman diseñó el plan de mediación de este proyecto y es el encargado de llevarlo a cabo. En estos dos años, han desarrollado actividades de vinculación con colegios a los que han ido a visitar con los elementos del cine fílmico, así como también han recibido a los establecimientos que han solicitado visitar el archivo.

En agosto del 2025, Olivares y Cayuman viajaron hasta Punta Arenas para ser parte del XVII Festival Internacional de Cine Polo Sur Latinoamericano con talleres y exhibiciones. Han realizado muestras de cine en la universidad con la presencia de personas relevantes del mundo documental y los archivos, como la antropóloga y documentalista mexicana Gabriela Zamorano y el estreno en Temuco de su documental Archivo Cordero, sobre uno de los mayores acervos visuales del siglo XX en Bolivia.

Otras de las actividades de mediación, fue Filmoteca Lab, en junio del 2026, que contó “con la presencia de investigadoras/es, cineastas y una gran cantidad de personas que se interesan por el uso de los archivos a nivel de la memoria local, de los procesos de creación artística, de los intereses disciplinares como la antropología, la geografía, y la educación”, señaló Ange Cayuman, agregando que “ha sido un proceso que ha abierto posibilidades de vinculación desde la universidad con el territorio que habita y otros, y de generación de investigación y creación, que es el fin de …

author: Rizomatica
title: “Los pueblos originarios hemos vivido la violencia sistemática por defender la vida y la naturaleza»: Onésima Lienqueo, candidata mapuche a Escazú
content:
La

Secretaría de Escazú

 recibió

candidaturas

 de 22 países para representar al público en el Acuerdo de Escazú, de las cuales 106 fueron admitidas. Entre ellas destaca la de

Onésima Lienqueo

, mujer mapuche, educadora y fundadora de

Enraizar

, con una importante trayectoria en la defensa de los derechos humanos, quien llama a fortalecer la protección de defensores ambientales y la participación de pueblos originarios, niñeces y mujeres indígenas.


Por: Equipo Comunicaciones Mapuche


El proceso de candidaturas al Acuerdo de Escazú


La

Secretaría de Escazú en América Latina

 recibió

116 candidaturas

 de

22 países

 de América Latina y el Caribe para representar al público en el Acuerdo de Escazú, según informó la propia Secretaría. De las 116 candidaturas recibidas,

106 fueron aceptadas

 y

10 no fueron admitidas

 por incumplir los requisitos establecidos en el

artículo 7 del Reglamento de las elecciones

. La

Subregión 1

 está conformada por

Argentina, Bolivia, Brasil, Chile, Colombia, Ecuador, Paraguay, Perú, Uruguay y Venezuela

.


Cabe destacar que el

Acuerdo de Escazú

 es el

primer tratado ambiental de América Latina y el Caribe

, adoptado en

Costa Rica el 4 de marzo de 2018

, que protege de manera específica a los

defensores de los derechos humanos ambientales

.

Chile es Estado Parte desde septiembre de 2022

, implementándolo mediante organismos como el

Ministerio del Medio Ambiente

 y el

Servicio de Evaluación Ambiental

.


La candidatura de Onésima Lienqueo


Entre las candidaturas aceptadas está la de

Onésima Lienqueo

, destacada defensora de los derechos de

niños, niñas y adolescentes (NNA)

 , defensora de derechos humanos y educadora. Al presentar su candidatura, Lienqueo señaló: «

Presento mi candidatura a representante del público del Acuerdo de Escazú desde una trayectoria de más de catorce años dedicada a la promoción y defensa de los derechos humanos, los derechos de los pueblos indígenas y la protección de quienes defienden la tierra, el territorio y el medio ambiente. Postulo también desde mi identidad como mujer mapuche, educadora, defensora, lideresa y vocera de procesos de defensa territorial, con la convicción de que la implementación efectiva del Acuerdo requiere una representación cercana a las comunidades y conectada con las realidades que viven las personas defensoras en América Latina y el Caribe

«.


Lienqueo es fundadora de

Enraizar

 y directora de su

Programa de Seguridad Holística para Personas Defensoras de Derechos Humanos y del Medio Ambiente

. Desde este espacio, señala:

«acompañamos a personas que enfrentan amenazas y distintas formas de violencia por proteger sus comunidades, sus territorios y los bienes comunes. Nuestro enfoque comprende la seguridad de manera integral, incorporando las dimensiones física, digital, emocional y colectiva, así como el autocuidado, la evaluación de riesgos y la construcción de redes de apoyo».


Lienqueo ha elaborado informes de denuncia, diagnósticos y evaluaciones de riesgo de personas defensoras en Chile, y ha colaborado en informes sobre la situación nacional relacionada con el Acuerdo de Escazú y sobre las realidades específicas de las mujeres defensoras.


Entrevista a Onésima Lienqueo


1.- ¿Por qué es importante la presencia de Pueblos Originarios en esta instancia de Escazú?

R:

 Es fundamental la participación de los Pueblos Originarios en estas instancias de participación, información y justicia.

Los pueblos originarios somos quienes hemos vivido la violencia sistemática por defender la vida y la naturaleza

, además de ser quienes preservamos en el mundo la mayor parte de la conservación de la naturaleza. Creo que como mujeres e indígenas debemos tener una representación que facilite, informe, comunique y represente la visión de nuestros pueblos ante el cuidado y protección de la

ñuke mapu

.


2.- ¿Cuál es el diagnóstico con respecto a la situación de defensores ambientales en Latam y Chile?

R:

 Latinoamérica enfrenta las más altas cifras de asesinatos y ataques a defensores ambientales,

Colombia y Brasil

 son quienes por varios años han tenido más muertes de personas defensoras.

Chile no queda excluido de esta violencia y riesgos por defender la tierra

, sin embargo los procesos son distintos ya que aquí se enfrentan ataques tales como la

title: Pourquoi et comment brûler la psychiatrie ? Discussion pour des perspectives antipsy anticarcérales
content:
Le mercredi 23 septembre 2026, l'Assemblée Anticarcérale Paris & Environs organise une discussion antipsychiatrie anticarcérale à la bibliothèque queer anarchiste la

BARK

, qui se trouve à la Parole Errante à Montreuil.


Mercredi 23 Septembre à 18h : Discussion antipsy anticarcérale à la

BARK

 

!


Depuis son lancement, l'Assemblée Anticarcérale Paris & Environs s'efforce de s'organiser contre l'enfermement psychiatrique. La psychiatrie nous apparaît naturellement comme un maillon important de la domination : que ce soit par les moyens par lesquels elle enferme des personnes, par son utilisation répressive et pacificatrice dans les autres lieux d'enfermement, ou par ses dispositifs carcéraux de contrôle dans la société. Dans une optique de s'informer sur les luttes contre la psychiatrie et d'y intervenir, on veut prendre en compte le fait que nous n'avons pas toustes les mêmes expériences et connaissances sur le sujet.


L'idée de cette discussion est donc de poser des bases, ensemble, sur ce qu'est l'antipsy pour nous, que ce soit pour découvrir ses courants ou pour développer ce qui nous parle dedans. Quels sont les dispositifs d'enfermement de la psychiatrie

 

? Pourquoi viser à sa destruction

 

? Quels liens faisons-nous depuis nos perspectives anticarcérales

 

? Comment la domination psychiatrique est elle étendue ces dernières années

 

? Comment s'organiser pour la brûler

 

?


Une base d'infokiosque sera aussi proposée pour approfondir certaines questions spécifiques, mais il ne faut pas hésiter à apporter toute brochure que l'on voudrait discuter, conseiller, diffuser, etc.


La discussion commencera dès 18h à la bibliothèque queer anarchiste la

BARK

 (5 rue francois debergue à la Parole Errante à Montreuil, en passant par le jardin à gauche de la librairie Michèle Firk). La permanence de la bibliothèque commence elle dès 16h, et l'infokiosque y sera installé en avance

 

!

author: Rana Mamdouh
title: Future of Egypt enters healthcare: Govt, military hospitals to serve tourist dollars
content:
In its first public move into the healthcare sector, the Future of Egypt for Sustainable Development Authority

unveiled

 last week the launch of the Future of Egypt Medical Alliance Company.


According to reports announcing the authority’s participation in this year’s Egy Health Exhibition and Conference, the company is chaired by Major General Khaled Oweida, the physician and former director of the Air Force Specialized Hospital, and is set to provide specialized medical services, training and research, digital and technological healthcare solutions, as well as medical tourism services.


In the first phase of its operations, the reports stated, the company will incorporate the International Medical Center and the Air Force Specialized Hospital, both of which are affiliated with the Armed Forces. The two facilities provide medical services to military personnel through the Armed Forces’ health insurance system, while also treating civilians for a fee or through

contracts

 with the Universal Health Insurance system or other entities.


The company plans to expand gradually by bringing additional facilities and hospitals under its umbrella.


This year’s Egy Health Exhibition and Conference, held September 15-17. Courtesy: Menassat website


Future of Egypt

also announced

 that the company was taking part in the exhibition, which was held from September 15 to 17, in order to “showcase its integrated medical system’s components and the range of specialties, services and advanced solutions it offers.”


Coverage of the exhibition focused on what media outlets described as the Future of Egypt Medical Alliance Company’s vision for developing medical tourism — mapping the international patient journey that runs from pre-travel consultations and case assessment, through travel, reception, accommodation and translation, to post-treatment follow-up.


According to media

coverage

, the company intends to pursue this by building a network of medical partners and tourism operators and establishing cooperation channels with entities involved in medical tourism and target markets.


Steps to foster a state vision for medical tourism date back to at least 2017, when Prime Minister Mostafa Madbuly

established

 the Supreme Committee for Medical Tourism by decree to be headed by the health minister. The decree set out several objectives, including implementing the medical tourism components of the Egypt Vision 2030, restoring the confidence of foreign patients, attracting Arab and foreign investment to establish projects serving medical tourism and involving civil society and the private sector.


During a committee meeting in December 2024, chaired by Madbuly, Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar

said

 the committee’s technical secretariat had begun preparing a unified national strategy for medical tourism. According to a Cabinet

statement

, the committee had contacted all relevant entities involved in health tourism in Egypt to solicit their proposals for the strategy.


At the same meeting, Madbuly said that it was agreed to establish a national council for medical tourism, with a technical secretariat tasked with following up on all matters related to this portfolio.


The council was established by a prime ministerial decree in June 2025. In its first meeting,

chaired

by the health minister, a proposal setting out criteria for service providers to join the national health tourism platform was reviewed. The providers included healthcare, hotel and hospitality, transportation and logistics services.


A senior Health Ministry official told Mada Masr on condition of anonymity that the Future of Egypt Medical Alliance Company is primarily focused on providing treatment to tourists: “[The company] is targeting Gulf nationals and foreign tourists in Egypt whose treatment costs are paid in dollars by international insurance companies.”


As an example, the official said, “if we perform open heart surgery for LE200,000 for someone insured in Egypt, [Future of Egypt’s] hospitals would perform the same operation for a foreign tourist staying in, say, Sharm el-Sheikh, and their insurance company would pay US$10,000. And we benefit from the difference in the exchange rate.”


According to the official, one of the main criteria for selecting hospitals to be transferred to Future of Egypt is having a helipad equipped to receive emergency cases, as well as facilities equipped for major surgeries and subspeciality medical care …

author: Dominic Gutoman
title: On The Fringes | Mentally surviving the rotten healthcare system
content:
Flower blooming outside the state mental health facility. Photo by Dominic Gutoman/Bulatlat.

I refer to the force pinning me down to the sofa. For hours, I negotiated with my own body and mind, trying to gather enough courage to leave the house and go to the public mental health facility.

The last time I was here, the queue was so long that it took seven hours to see the doctor. As the body ached in intense abdominal pain, I tried not to cave in. Today, I arrived at past seven in the morning and I was No. 40. I managed to get a seat. That is already a small victory for the expected long day.

Most patients need to be accompanied. I am fortunate that I can still do this on my own.

There is a certain kind of fortitude required to spend an entire day waiting in a public hospital. But this “strength” is a product of a decaying public healthcare, of a system designed to make people used to surviving what should never have been normal. When the system designed to care for us is also pulling us down, this “strength” is dangerous.

In this hospital, only one psychiatrist is assigned for all patients. This explains the hours of long lines of patients every day.

Based on a 2026 study of University of the Philippines, there are 409 PhilHealth-accredited psychiatrists in the country, translating to 0.38 psychiatrists per 100,000 population. It also noted that the country’s ratio of psychiatrists and population has been decreasing since 2016. This shortage is not only about numbers but also about people’s access to health services.

If people struggling with their mental health opt for private consultations, the average cost ranges from P1,500 ($23.89) to P5,000 ($79.63) per session.

For the poor who are forced to join the long lines, the cost of psychiatric care is not an incidental expense. It can deprive families of food for several days, not to mention money allocated for utility bills, transportation, and rent.

The situation is much worse for minimum wage earners or contractual employees living from paycheck to paycheck. Sacrificing one whole day to get immediate psychiatric care means income loss.

Think tank Ibon Foundation said that around 70 million Filipinos belong to the poorest and low-income classes, earning between P10,000 ($159.27) and P22,000 ($350.39) monthly.

The high cost of consultation left poor patients to rely on a rotten public mental health system. Of course, the shame and stigma tend to prevent people from seeking psychiatric help.

The 2023 data from the Department of Health (DOH) showed that more than 3.6 million Filipinos suffer from mental health conditions, neurological and substance use disorders. Among the most prevalent conditions are major depressive disorder (affecting more than 1.1 million people); bipolar disorder (520,000 people); and schizophrenia (more than 213,000 people).

Behind all these numbers is the long line right now, with me sitting on a worn out chair in the waiting area. Someone is constantly checking the clock. Someone is wondering if the doctor will see him before the day ends. And someone is trying not to give up in this dreadful wait.

I had the privilege to take a leave at work to prioritize my consultation. But an average Filipino worker does not have this privilege, especially minimum wage earners and the contractual workers trapped in a no-work-no-pay system.

It’s already 3:00 pm. The two bottles of water and three pieces of bread are gone. The cellphone battery is running low.

A first-time outpatient tells another that it took her a long time to finally bring herself here. “Because of shame,” she said.

Behind her, a woman in her 50s told her, “You shouldn’t be ashamed. We are all survivors.” Sitting in the waiting area for half a day, most of us heard several stories of survival.

We pretended not to listen. But we heard such stories. This explains why the waiting area is difficult to forget. I spent more hours here than in my consultations. Most of my conversations with the doctor took only 15 to 30 minutes.

It’s 4:00 pm now, almost nine hours of waiting. I am already next in line. I may not be a doctor and I may be struggling but it is clear that the public healthcare system is dying from decay. (RTS, DAA)

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Warren Introduces Bill to Ban Private Equity From Owning Medical Practices
content:
More than 80 percent of doctors are employed by corporate entities — a massive increase from 62 percent seven years ago.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

A group of Democrats has introduced bicameral legislation to ban private equity from owning medical practices as increasingly widespread corporate ownership continues driving up health care costs each year.

The bill was introduced Wednesday by Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Massachusetts) with the support of 12 other members of the Senate and House. The legislation was based on a law in Oregon aimed at beating back the corporate takeover of health care providers that took effect this year. The law has already been successfully used by physicians in Eugene to prevent a corporate takeover.

Warren’s bill would ban for-profit corporations like private equity funds and insurance companies from owning medical practices, while also prohibiting entities known as management services organizations, which conduct business operations for practices, from controlling such offices.

Such a prohibition could help stanch the rapid rise in health care costs. Between 2000 and 2004, KFF found, costs for medical care far outpaced costs for goods and services at large, increasing by 121 percent compared to 86 percent for the rest of the consumer price index.

The growing grip of private equity on health care, like in other sectors, has played a major role in this rise in costs. In 2000, private equity invested $5 billion in health care; by 2024, this had risen to $104 billion. Since private equity firms are focused not on patient care, but on maximizing profits, research has found that private equity ownership is associated with worse outcomes for patients as well as higher costs, particularly in nursing homes.

In large part due to rising costs for care, health coverage costs are slated to rise precipitously next year. A recent survey found that employers expect health care plan costs to rise by an average of 11 percent per worker in 2027, unless benefits are cut. This could translate to higher costs for workers and patients on job-based insurance if employers shift the burden onto them; costs for plans through the Affordable Care Act are also expected to rise significantly due to Republicans’ massive slashes via the One Big Beautiful Bill.

“Patients want to know that decisions about their health are being made by their doctors, not by Wall Street investors,” said Warren. “If we’re going to lower costs and un-rig the health care system, we need to stop the corporate takeover of medicine.”

The passage of the bill could also help allow physicians to retain control in their practices, including in their medical decisionmaking, at a time when private equity and other corporate actors are close to gobbling up almost the entire field of medical providers.

As the lawmakers point out, research has found that, as of this year, 82 percent of physicians are employed by hospitals or other corporate entities as the industry shifts away from private practices. This is a 20-point increase from 2019, when 62 percent of physicians were employed this way.

The legislation has been backed by numerous health and advocacy groups, who say that private equity must be barred from standing between patients and receiving good health care.

“A prohibition is only as strong as its enforcement, and this bill backs its corporate practice of medicine prohibition with three enforcement paths: the FTC, state attorneys general suing on behalf of residents, and physicians themselves through a private right of action with treble damages,” said Marco Fernandez, president of the Association for Independent Medicine. “That layered enforcement, paired with mandatory divestment, is what gives this bill teeth that earlier [Corporate Practice of Medicine] laws have often lacked.”

title: The Saddle Lake Cree Nation, located northeast of Edmonton near St. Paul, says health care is a…
content:
The Saddle Lake Cree Nation, located northeast of Edmonton near St. Paul, says health care is a right under Treaty 6 and falls under its inherent jurisdiction. The First Nation has invoked the “medicine chest clause” provision from the treaty signed in 1876, which Indigenous Peoples interpret as a promise to provide comprehensive health care. “All children, including trans and two-spirit children and their family, will have safety under our treaty,” Saddle Lake Chief Dale Steinhauer said on Wednesday.

author: Arezu Fayyazi
title: No Girls and women in Classrooms. No Women in Health Clinics. Afghanistan’s Healthcare Crisis Deepens by the Day.
content:
It has been five years since women and girls in Afghanistan have been among the primary targets of the Taliban regime. Their rights to go to school, go to work, and even leave their homes have been taken away. A direct consequence of these restrictions is a crumbling health system, under pressure from a lack of female medical professionals, Taliban restrictions, and funding cuts that threaten to keep health facilities open.

One of the first Taliban orders was to ban women from pursuing higher education and to ban all girls from attending school beyond grade six. According to UNICEF, more than 2.6 million girls do not have access to education as a result of the Taliban’s ban. Other edicts target women’s freedom of movement, including restrictions that prevent women from leaving their homes or going to health clinics without a male family member. These edicts have built on one another to the point where Afghanistan’s education and health systems are being systematically dismantled. The pipeline that once supplied the workforce with trained and skilled professionals is disappearing, creating major long-term consequences for the health system and the country’s workforce.

Due to this dismantled pipeline, Afghanistan is facing one of the worst shortages of female medical professionals. In Helmand, Zabul, and Uruzgan provinces, it is reported that there are no female medical professionals. There are only three female specialists in Kandahar, a neighboring province to Helmand. In addition to specialists, other female healthcare workers that Afghanistan’s health system depends on, such as midwives and nurses, have been forced out of their jobs because of Taliban restrictions. And because of restrictions on movement, Afghan women are also unable to visit health facilities and obtain treatment, according to a February 2026 report by UN Special Rapporteur Richard Bennett.

The cost of the ban on education and the removal of women from the workforce also has a deep and lasting economic impact. It is estimated that this will cost Afghanistan $84 million per year. But beyond the economic impact, the immediate human consequences are even more urgent. Infant and maternal mortality have risen back to some of the highest levels seen since the Taliban took over.

The lack of specialists, and in some areas any female healthcare workers at all, means that women are facing a painful reality. An Afghan from Helmand shared, “We take patients from one doctor to another without success and eventually have to go elsewhere.”

Manizha, a medical doctor whose name has been changed for her safety, is part of one of the few medical teams still providing care to Afghan women. She sees women who would otherwise have no access to healthcare, with her team traveling to them. Her team originally started with fourteen members, but has since decreased to seven, as many of her colleagues were unable to find male guardians to accompany them to work, compounded by financial hardships.

With decreasing staff and an increasing health burden, the situation is dire. Even as Manizha faces enormous challenges, she remains hopeful: “Whenever I remember the smiles, the tears, and even the deprivation of the women I have visited over the years, I tell myself that I must not give up. They need even the little that I can do for them.”

Afghanistan’s healthcare system is collapsing because the foundation of a skilled labor force including women is collapsing. By excluding women from education, employment, and public life, the Taliban are not only denying women their rights today; they are dismantling the pipeline needed to train the healthcare professionals Afghanistan will need tomorrow. The result is a health system that is losing its existing female workforce while failing to produce the next generation of women professionals to serve their communities.

Sources: Feminist Majority Foundation, Afghanistan International, United Nations, UNICEF, Rukhshana

title: İstanbul Barosu’ndan engelli çocukların eğitim hakkı için veli rehberi
content:
İstanbul Barosu Engelli Hakları Merkezi, yeni eğitim-öğretim döneminde engelli çocukların ve ailelerinin okullarda karşılaşabileceği hak ihlallerine karşı 

“Eğitimde Sağlamcılığa Hayır! Engelli Çocukların Eğitim Hakkı İçin Veli Rehberi”

 başlıklı bir çalışma yayımladı.


Eylül 2026 tarihli 68 sayfalık rehber; okul kaydı, sağlık raporu talepleri, “gölge öğretmen” dayatması, başka okula ya da sınıfa yönlendirme, Bireyselleştirilmiş Eğitim Programı (BEP), destek eğitim odası, erişilebilirlik, yardımcı cihazlar, akran zorbalığı, ayrımcılık ve mahremiyet gibi başlıkları ele alıyor. Ailelerin sorun yaşaması halinde başvurabileceği idari ve hukuki yollar ile örnek dilekçeler de rehberde yer alıyor.


“Çözüm çocuğu eğitim ortamından uzaklaştırmak değil”


Rehberde öne çıkan sorunlardan biri, engelli çocukların okul kaydı sırasında karşılaştığı doğrudan ya da dolaylı ret uygulamaları.


Baro, bir çocuğun engelli olmasının tek başına okul kaydının reddedilmesi için gerekçe oluşturamayacağını hatırlatıyor. Okulların “Bu okul çocuğunuza uygun değil”, “Sınıf çok kalabalık”, “Öğretmenimiz bu konuda eğitimli değil” ya da “Başka okul daha iyi olur” gibi gerekçelerle çocuğu eğitim ortamından uzaklaştırmasının eğitim hakkını ortadan kaldırmadığını belirtiyor.


Engelli Odaklı Habercilik Atölyesi sona erdi: "Kafamızdaki sağlamcıyı öldürmeliyiz"


25 Haziran 2026


“Gölge öğretmen tutamazsanız okula alamayız” denilemez


Rehberin dikkat çektiği uygulamalardan biri de bazı ailelerden çocuklarının okula devam edebilmesi için kendi imkanlarıyla “gölge öğretmen” ya da destek personeli sağlamalarının istenmesi.


İstanbul Barosu, çocuğun sınıf içinde desteğe ihtiyaç duyması halinde öncelikle BEP, destek eğitim ve sınıf içi uyarlamalar gibi kamusal yükümlülüklerin değerlendirilmesi gerektiğini vurguluyor.


Ailenin ekonomik gücüyle özel bir personel çalıştırabilmesi ile çocuğun anayasal eğitim hakkının birbirine karıştırılamayacağını belirten rehber, okul kabulünün ailenin ücretini ödeyeceği bir personel bulmasına bağlanmasının eğitim hakkı ve ayrımcılık yasağı bakımından ciddi hukuki sorun doğurabileceğine dikkat çekiyor.


Okul yönetimi tek başına “Bu çocuk bu sınıfta yapamaz” diyemez


Baro ayrıca, engelli bir öğrencinin başka okula veya özel eğitim sınıfına gönderilmesine yalnızca öğretmenin ya da okul yönetiminin karar veremeyeceğini hatırlatıyor.


Çocuğun eğitim ortamının değiştirilmesinin eğitsel değerlendirme ve tanılama sürecine bağlı olduğu; değerlendirmelerin Rehberlik ve Araştırma Merkezi (RAM) bünyesindeki kurul tarafından yapılması gerektiği belirtiliyor.


Yerleştirme kararında velinin yazılı talebinin de dikkate alınması gerekiyor. Bu nedenle öğretmenin ya da okul müdürünün “Bu çocuk burada yapamaz” şeklindeki değerlendirmesinin tek başına yerleştirme kararı sayılamayacağı ifade ediliyor.


Engelsiz Erişim Derneği: Otizm “farkındalık” değil, kabul ve eşit erişim meselesi


2 Nisan 2026


Destek eğitim odası çocuğu sınıftan uzaklaştırmanın aracı değil


Rehber, tam zamanlı kaynaştırma/bütünleştirme yoluyla eğitim gören öğrenciler bakımından destek eğitim odalarına da geniş yer ayırıyor.


Destek eğitim odasında verilecek eğitimin öğrencinin haftalık toplam ders saatinin yüzde 40'ını aşamayacağı; temel olarak bire bir yürütüleceği, BEP geliştirme biriminin kararıyla en fazla üç öğrenciden oluşan gruplarla da eğitim yapılabileceği aktarılıyor.


Ancak rehber özellikle bir noktaya dikkat çekiyor: Destek eğitim odası, öğrenciyi akranlarından soyutlamak veya genel eğitim sınıfından uzaklaştırmak için kullanılamaz.


Okul yönetiminin “odamız yok” ya da “öğretmenimiz yok” demesinin de tek başına öğrencinin ihtiyaç duyduğu desteğin karşılanmamasını hukuken haklı hale getirmeyeceği belirtiliyor.


Zorbalığa karşı önlem almak okulun yükümlülüğü


Çalışmanın “Güvenli okul, ayrımcılık ve mahremiyet” bölümünde engelli çocukların karşılaşabileceği akran zorbalığı da ele alınıyor.


Alay etme, hakaret, tehdit, dışlama, fiziksel şiddet, çocuğun eşyalarına veya kullandığı yardımcı cihazlara müdahale ve dijital ortamda rahatsız etme zorbalığın farklı biçimleri arasında sayılıyor.


Rehber, Milli Eğitim Bakanlığı'nın ilgili genelgelerine işaret ederek okul yönetimlerinin zorbalığa yol açabilecek riskleri belirlemek, önleyici tedbir almak ve rehberlik hizmetlerini işletmekle yükümlü olduğunu hatırlatıyor.


Ailelere her bir olayı tarih, yer ve gerçekleşme biçimiyle ayrı ayrı kaydetmeleri öneriliyor.

title: Şiddetten kaçan engelli kadın için sığınma evine ulaşmak daha zor: Erişilebilir bina yetmez, erişilebilir sığınma hizmeti ihtiyaç
content:
Şiddete maruz bırakılan bir kadın evinden ayrılmaya karar verdiğinde güvenli bir yere ulaşabilmek için çoğu zaman polis, Şiddet Önleme ve İzleme Merkezi (ŞÖNİM), belediyelerin danışma birimleri veya destek hatlarıyla iletişime geçmek zorunda. Ancak bu süreç, her kadın için aynı ölçüde erişilebilir değil. Kadın engelliyse şiddetten uzaklaşmanın önündeki engellere; erişilemeyen binalar, iletişim kanallarındaki sorunlar, işaret dili desteğinin bulunmaması, kişisel bakım ihtiyacının karşılanmaması ve ayrımcı kabuller de ekleniyor.

Aile ve Sosyal Hizmetler Bakanlığının 2025 Yılı Faaliyet Raporu’na göre Türkiye’de bakanlığa, yerel yönetimlere, bir sivil toplum kuruluşuna ve Göç İdaresi Başkanlığı’na bağlı toplam 151 kadın konukevi bulunuyor. 3 bin 726 kapasiteli bu kuruluşlar, aynı yıl kadınlar ve beraberlerindeki çocuklar dâhil 62 bin 698 kişiye hizmet sundu. Türkiye genelindeki 86 ŞÖNİM’e yapılan başvuru sayısı ise 310 bin 136 olarak kayda geçti.

Ancak Bakanlığın raporunda kadın konukevlerine başvuran veya bu kuruluşlardan yararlanan engelli kadınların sayısı, engel grupları, kabul ve yönlendirme süreçleri ayrı ayrı açıklanmıyor. Dolayısıyla kritik sorular yanıtsız kalıyor: Kaç engelli kadın sığınma talebinde bulundu? Kaçı kabul edildi? Kaçı öz bakım veya iletişim desteği sağlanamadığı için başka bir kuruma yönlendirildi? Avukat Deniz Yazgan’a göre veri eksikliği, ayrımcılığın boyutunu da görünmez hâle getiriyor: “Hangi engel gruplarında ret veya yönlendirme yoğunlaşıyor? Hangi makul düzenlemeler talep ediliyor ve bunların ne kadarı karşılanıyor?”

Mor Çatı Gönüllüsü Kübra Karagöz ise engelli kadınların karşılaştığı sorunların çoğu zaman sığınağın kapısından içeri girmeden başladığına işaret etti. Mevcut sistemde kadınlar konukevine doğrudan başvuramıyor. İl müdürlüğü, ŞÖNİM, ilgili kamu birimleri veya kolluk aracılığıyla yönlendirme yapılıyor. Bu nedenle ilk temas kurulan görevlinin yaklaşımı, doğru bilgi vermesi ve süreci geciktirmeden yürütmesi büyük önem taşıyor.

Karagöz, kadınların bu süreçte zaman zaman şiddetin nedenine ilişkin sorgulayıcı yorumlar, küçümseme, caydırıcı ifadeler ve sığınaklar hakkında yanlış bilgilendirmeyle karşılaştığını belirtti. Engelli kadınlar söz konusu olduğunda ise bu tutumların daha da ağırlaşabildiğine dikkat çekti. Ayrıca kadınların “engelli bir kadın olarak sığınakta kalmasının zor olacağı” yönünde bilgilendirilebildiğini, hatta bazı kadınlara sığınaklara engelli kadın kabul edilmediğinin söylendiğini aktardı.

Bu tablo, erişilebilirliğin yalnızca sığınak binasının girişindeki rampadan ibaret olmadığını gösteriyor. Bir kadın yardım hattına ulaşamıyor, telefonda iletişim kuramıyor, kendisine sunulan bilgiyi anlayabileceği biçimde alamıyor veya güvenli ulaşım desteği bulamıyorsa, bina fiziksel olarak erişilebilir olsa bile koruma zinciri daha ilk aşamada kopuyor. Bazı kadınlar ise engeller nedeniyle destek alamayacaklarını düşünerek hiçbir mekanizmaya başvurmuyor.

Mor Çatı’ya ulaşan kadınların anlatımları, sığınaklar arasında da ortak ve yerleşik bir standardın bulunmadığını gösteriyor. Koşulların yalnızca kentten kente değil, aynı kentteki farklı sığınaklar arasında dahi değişebildiği belirtiliyor. Bazı kadınlar saat ve telefon kullanımına ilişkin kısıtlamalar ile bina içindeki düzenlemeler nedeniyle sığınakları “hapishaneye” benzetirken, bazıları iyi koşullarla karşılaşabiliyor.

Oturmuş bir standart olmadığı için ana dilde destek, işaret dili desteği ya da erişilebilirlik konusunda kapsayıcı bir çalışma olmadığını ifade eden Karagöz, bununla birlikte olumlu örneklerin de bulunduğunu aktardı. Bazı durumlarda engelli kadınların ilk kabulde daha kısa sürede yerleştirildiğini ve çocuklarıyla tek başına kalabilecekleri bir odaya yerleştirildiklerini söyleyen Karagöz, “Ancak bu uygulama tüm sığınaklarda yok” dedi.

Avukat ve Engelli Kadın Derneği Yönetim Kurulu Üyesi Özlem Kara’nın anlatımına göre; engellilik ve destek ilişkisi fail tarafından yeni kontrol araçlarına dönüştürülebiliyor. Tekerlekli sandalye, beyaz baston, işitme cihazı veya iletişim aracının saklanması; ilaç, beslenme, tuvalet, hijyen ve kişisel bakım desteğinin kasten engellenmesi; engelli aylığına veya banka hesabına el konulması bu şiddet biçimleri arasında. Telefon, internet, işaret dili tercümanı, Braille (görme engelliler için alfabe) veya kolay okunur bilgiye erişimin engellenmesi de kadını ihbar ve destek mekanizmalarından koparabiliyor. Failin aynı zamanda bakım veren kişi olması ise şiddet ortamından …

title: Nurses Across US Demand Hospitals Cut Ties With Palantir, Citing ICE and Gaza
content:
National Nurses United is expanding its campaign against Palantir in a global week of action starting on September 28.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

National Nurses United (NNU), the largest union of registered nurses in the U.S., is demanding that hospitals cut ties with Palantir, with nurses citing the firm’s role in developing technology used to surveil immigrants in the U.S. and target civilians in Gaza.

The union – which represents more than 225,000 nurses in all 50 U.S. states — has announced a global week of action against Palantir, set to begin on September 28.

Palantir’s “AI-powered tools for large-scale data collection and mass surveillance… threaten human rights globally,” the union said in a press release announcing the campaign.

The global week of action is aimed at pushing all public institutions — including hospitals and other health care providers — to end contracts and partnerships with Palantir, and to divest from the company, the union said.

The global week of action builds on a national day of action, also led by the union, which saw demonstrations in eight cities across the U.S. on August 27, including in Portland, Maine; Washington, D.C.; Chicago; Austin; and Los Angeles.

The global week of action is also coordinated with health care workers in the U.K., where National Health Service (NHS) workers and activists will protest Palantir’s use in health care on October 1. Other organizations, like Amnesty International and the Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions (BDS) Movement, are also part of the global week of action.

“Palantir has no place in patient care, no place in our communities, and no place in our society,” a NNU nurse said in a video from the August 27 day of action.

The nurses have outlined Palantir’s complicity in human rights violations both nationally and internationally, from detentions of immigrants by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to the genocide in Gaza.

“We think that a company that specializes in mass surveillance, kidnappings and killings, has no place in patient care,” one nurse explained in a video posted by the California Nurses Association.

During the August day of action, nurses placed 50 pairs of baby shoes in the street in each city – to represent the 500 babies and toddlers who have been detained in immigrant jails since President Donald Trump started his second term. The nurses also brought letters written by children in ICE detention.

“Palantir, we know, helps ICE identify people to kidnap off of our streets,” another nurse said during the day of action.

The company also has “their hands in the genocide and murders of civilians in Gaza,” another nurse present at the protests said. “They’ve [helped with the targeting of] hospitals, schools, mission workers taking food and aid….”

In a statement shared with Truthout and read at the August 27 day of action, Chicago-based nurse and NNU member Elizabeth Lalasz said that “nurses, health care workers, our patients, immigrants, and allies from every walk of life stand united here in Chicago and all across the country to demand an immediate end to the violence inflicted by Palantir technologies and the Trump administration.”

“As we speak, Palantir’s AI is enabling atrocities and human rights abuses: ICE killings, mass deportation, and concentration camps with no access to health care – even the imprisonment of more than 500 babies and 6,200 children – and Palantir is providing the technology for Israel’s U.S.-funded genocide in Gaza, the cruel and illegal war in Iran, and mass surveillance at home and abroad,” she went on.

Lalasz also noted that Palantir has partnered with the world’s largest health care corporations “to suck more and more profit from our broken health care system, causing untold suffering in our hospitals.”

“This country could fund health care for 12 million children with the money spent on ICE detention alone,” she said.

João Paulo Connolly, an activist in the Bay Area who has organized protests against Palantir, explained in a webinar that “Palantir’s profit model is data extraction and surveillance,” and then “giving employers new, powerful ways to monitor and spy on their workers at all times and track their behavior,” while also selling the health care industry and the federal government “unprecedented levels of access” to this data.
